questions.q: What does the symbol µm stand for, and what is it equal to in metres?
questions.e: µm stands for micrometre, equal to 10⁻⁶ m (one millionth of a metre) — the standard unit for whole-cell sizes.

questions.q: A nanometre (nm) is equal to how many metres?
questions.e: 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m, one billionth of a metre — used for organelles, membranes and viruses.

questions.q: How many nanometres are there in 1 micrometre?
questions.e: Since 1 µm = 10⁻⁶ m and 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m, 1 µm = 1000 nm.

questions.q: The Angstrom (Å) unit is equal to how many metres?
questions.e: 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m, used to describe atomic- and molecular-scale distances such as the width of a DNA helix.

questions.q: How many Angstroms (Å) make up 1 nanometre?
questions.e: 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m and 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m, so 1 nm = 10 Å.

questions.q: Which unit would be most appropriate for describing the diameter of a typical animal cell (about 10–30 across)?
questions.e: Whole cells are conveniently expressed in micrometres (µm); nanometres and Angstroms are reserved for much smaller structures.

questions.q: What is a simple microscope?
o: A microscope with two lenses in series
A microscope with no lenses, using only mirrors
A microscope using a single lens system
A microscope that only works with fluorescent stains
questions.e: A simple microscope magnifies using a single lens system, such as a magnifying glass or loupe.

questions.q: Who first coined the term "cell" after examining thin slices of cork tissue?
questions.e: Robert Hooke examined cork under a microscope in 1665 and named the small box-like compartments he saw "cells."

questions.q: Robert Hooke's cork observations were actually of what?
o: Empty cell walls left behind by dead plant tissue
Animal cells from a specimen slide
questions.e: The cork Hooke examined was dead tissue, so what he saw and named "cells" were the empty cell walls, not living cell contents.

questions.q: Which scientist ground his own single-lens microscopes and was the first to observe living microorganisms, which he called "animalcules"?
questions.e: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek built powerful simple (single-lens) microscopes and was the first to describe bacteria and protozoa, which he termed "animalcules."

questions.q: Van Leeuwenhoek's "animalcules" correspond to which modern groups of organisms?
questions.e: His animalcules were what we now recognise as bacteria and protozoa — the first living microorganisms ever described.

questions.q: A loupe (hand lens) is best described as which type of instrument?
o: A compound microscope with two lens systems
An electron microscope for atomic resolution
A dissecting microscope with two optical paths
A simple magnifier using a single convex lens
questions.e: A loupe is a simple magnifier — a single small convex lens held close to the eye — the direct descendant of van Leeuwenhoek's single-lens microscopes.

questions.q: Which of the following best distinguishes a simple microscope from a compound microscope?
o: A simple microscope uses one lens system; a compound microscope uses two
A simple microscope always has higher magnification
A simple microscope requires electricity to operate
A simple microscope can only view opaque specimens
questions.e: The defining difference is the number of lens systems: one for a simple microscope, two (eyepiece + objective) for a compound microscope.

questions.q: Why was Robert Hooke's naming of "cells" historically significant, even though he saw only cell walls?
o: It proved that all cells contain a nucleus, a claim the cork tissue itself could never have supported
It established the term still used today for the basic unit of life, launching cell biology as a field
It disproved van Leeuwenhoek's animalcule observations, ruling bacteria out as living cells entirely
It was the first use of an electron microscope, a technology not invented until centuries later
questions.e: Despite observing only dead cell walls, Hooke's coinage of "cell" gave biology the term still used for the basic structural unit of life.

questions.q: What is spherical aberration?
o: Different wavelengths of light focusing at different points along the optical axis of the lens
A crack forming gradually in the glass of the lens as it ages over years of use
Light rays through different parts of a spherical lens focusing at different points, blurring the image
The lens being ground into an imperfect sphere shape during manufacture, distorting the image
questions.e: Spherical aberration occurs because rays passing through the edge of a spherical lens focus at a different point than rays through the centre, blurring the image.

questions.q: Which of the following is a valid way to correct spherical aberration?
o: Using an achromatic doublet only, without addressing the shape of the lens surface itself
Increasing the light source's brightness, which changes contrast but not ray convergence
Removing the condenser entirely, which would in fact worsen illumination and image quality
Using a diaphragm/stop to block outer rays and use only the central part of the lens
questions.e: Restricting light to the central part of the lens with a diaphragm/stop reduces spherical aberration, along with oil immersion and compound lens systems.

questions.q: Besides using a diaphragm, which other methods help correct spherical aberration?
o: Oil immersion and compound lens systems
Reducing the working distance to zero
questions.e: Oil immersion and compound lens systems with aspherical surfaces are both used to reduce spherical aberration.

questions.q: What is chromatic aberration?
o: Loss of image brightness at high magnification as the objective's light cone narrows
Different wavelengths of light refracting by different amounts, causing colour fringing
Rays from the lens edge focusing differently from rays through the centre of the lens
The stage vibrating during observation, blurring the image through mechanical motion
questions.e: Chromatic aberration happens because a simple lens bends different wavelengths of light by different amounts, so colours focus at slightly different points, producing coloured fringes.

questions.q: How is chromatic aberration typically corrected in microscope lenses?
o: By using a diaphragm to block outer rays
By reducing the numerical aperture to zero
By using only monochromatic red light
questions.e: An achromatic lens, usually an achromatic doublet, corrects chromatic aberration by bringing different wavelengths to a common focus.

questions.q: An achromatic doublet is constructed from which combination of materials?
o: Two identical pieces of crown glass cemented together with no difference in refractive index
Plastic and quartz fused together, materials not actually used in doublet construction
A single piece of tinted glass, which cannot correct for wavelength-dependent focusing
A converging lens of crown glass cemented to a diverging lens of flint glass, with different refractive indices
questions.e: An achromatic doublet cements a crown-glass converging lens to a flint-glass diverging lens; their differing refractive indices/dispersion cancel out chromatic aberration.

questions.q: Which aberration is caused by rays passing through different regions of a lens's spherical surface, rather than by differences in wavelength?
questions.e: Spherical aberration is about ray position on the lens surface (edge vs. centre); chromatic aberration is about differences in wavelength.

questions.q: Why do modern microscope objectives (achromat, fluorite, apochromat) use multiple lens elements rather than a single lens?
o: Multiple elements are cheaper to manufacture than a single precision-ground aspherical lens element
Combining several lens elements helps correct both spherical and chromatic aberration together, sharpening the final image
A single lens element cannot magnify at all, which is not actually true of simple magnifying lenses
Multiple elements are required only for oil immersion objectives, never for dry low- or high-power ones
questions.e: Multi-element objective designs are engineered specifically to minimise both spherical and chromatic aberration simultaneously, producing a sharper image than a single lens ever could.

questions.q: A compound microscope gets its name because it combines which two lens systems along the light path?
o: The ocular lens and the objective lens
Two eyepieces with no objective lens
questions.e: A compound microscope combines an ocular (eyepiece) lens and an objective lens in series, multiplying their magnifying powers.

questions.q: What is the typical magnifying power range of a compound microscope's eyepiece (ocular)?
questions.e: Eyepieces are typically 10x or 15x magnifying power.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the light path through a compound microscope, from the light source to the eye?
o: Light source → condenser → specimen → objective → eyepiece → eye
Light source → objective → condenser → specimen → eyepiece → eye
Light source → specimen → condenser → objective → eyepiece → eye
Light source → eyepiece → objective → specimen → condenser → eye
questions.e: Light travels: light source → condenser (focuses light) → specimen → objective lens → eyepiece (ocular) → the observer's eye.

questions.q: What is the function of the nosepiece on a compound microscope?
o: It holds the specimen slide in place, a function actually performed by the stage clips
It is the rotating turret that holds the objective lenses and allows switching between them
It focuses light before it reaches the specimen, a function performed by the condenser
It is another name for the eyepiece, which actually sits at the top of the tube
questions.e: The nosepiece is the rotating turret mounted with the objective lenses, letting the user click between low power, high power and oil-immersion objectives.

questions.q: A typical compound microscope's set of objective lenses usually includes which combination?
o: Low power, high power, and oil-immersion objectives
One universal lens used for all magnifications
questions.e: Compound microscopes typically carry a set of objectives — low power, high power, and oil immersion — each offering a different magnification and NA.

questions.q: What is the role of the condenser in a compound microscope?
o: It rotates to switch between objective lenses, a function performed by the nosepiece
It magnifies the final image for the eye, a function performed by the eyepiece lens
It holds the slide flat on the stage, a function performed by the stage clips
It is a lens beneath the stage that focuses/concentrates light onto the specimen
questions.e: The condenser, positioned below the stage, focuses and concentrates light from the source onto the specimen.

questions.q: What does the iris diaphragm control on a compound microscope?
o: The amount of light and the width of the light cone reaching the specimen, affecting contrast and NA
The rotation speed of the nosepiece, which is turned by hand rather than by the diaphragm
The vertical height of the stage, which is instead adjusted by the focus knobs
The colour of the light source, which is instead set by filters or the bulb itself
questions.e: The iris diaphragm is an adjustable aperture that regulates how much light, and how wide a light cone, reaches the specimen — influencing both image contrast and numerical aperture.

questions.q: What is the difference in function between the coarse and fine focus knobs?
o: The coarse knob is used only for oil-immersion objectives, never for low or high power viewing
The coarse knob makes quick, large focusing movements; the fine knob makes small, precise adjustments for sharpness
The fine knob controls light intensity, a function actually performed by the diaphragm and lamp
There is no functional difference between them, so either knob can be used for every focusing step
questions.e: The coarse focus knob moves the stage/objective quickly for initial focusing, while the fine focus knob makes small, precise adjustments to sharpen the image.

questions.q: If a compound microscope has a 10x eyepiece and a 40x objective in use, what is the total magnification?
questions.e: Total magnification for a compound microscope = eyepiece power × objective power = 10 × 40 = 400x.

questions.q: A microscope described as "parfocal" means what?
o: It requires no focusing at all under any objective, once the specimen is first located
It can only be used with oil immersion, never with dry low- or high-power objectives
It automatically switches objectives, which actually still requires manual rotation
The image stays approximately in focus when switching between objectives of different magnification
questions.e: Parfocal means the image remains approximately in focus after rotating the nosepiece to a different-magnification objective, needing only minor fine-focus adjustment.

questions.q: Why should you always begin focusing a specimen using the lowest-power objective?
o: Because parfocal design means the image found at low power stays roughly in focus when switching to higher power objectives, making fine focusing easier and safer
Because low-power objectives cannot go out of focus once the coarse knob has first been used to roughly locate and centre the specimen on the stage
Because low power objectives require immersion oil before any higher power objective can ever be safely swapped into the rotating nosepiece
Because the condenser only works properly at low power and must always be swapped out before using any higher power objective lens
questions.e: Thanks to the parfocal property, starting at low power lets you locate and roughly focus the specimen, so only small fine-focus adjustments are needed at higher powers — reducing the risk of crashing the lens into the slide.

questions.q: What happens to the working distance as objective magnification increases?
o: It increases proportionally, giving more room between the lens and the specimen
It decreases — high-power and oil-immersion objectives sit very close to the specimen
It stays exactly the same at every magnification, regardless of the objective in use
It becomes undefined above 100x, a claim that does not match real objective design
questions.e: Working distance (the gap between the objective tip and the specimen) shrinks as magnification increases; oil-immersion objectives come extremely close to, and are optically coupled to, the slide.

questions.q: Which objective type has the shortest working distance, typically almost touching the specimen (via a film of oil)?
questions.e: Oil-immersion objectives have the shortest working distance of all, practically touching the specimen through the immersion oil layer.

questions.q: A dissecting (stereo) microscope is best suited for which type of specimen?
o: Thin, translucent specimens mounted on a slide under oil immersion at high power
Only bacterial smears requiring high magnification and fine resolving power
Only specimens viewed under UV light, which dissecting microscopes cannot provide
Larger or opaque specimens viewed whole, in three dimensions, at low magnification
questions.e: Dissecting microscopes are used for low-magnification, 3-D viewing of larger or opaque specimens that can't be thinly sliced onto a slide.

questions.q: What is the approximate maximum magnification of a typical dissecting (stereo) microscope?
questions.e: Dissecting microscopes are designed for low magnification, generally up to about 30x, prioritising working distance and 3-D view over fine detail.

questions.q: What gives a dissecting microscope its stereoscopic (3-D) view?
o: A single very powerful objective lens
Two separate optical paths, one for each eye
A rotating stage that spins the specimen
questions.e: A dissecting microscope has two separate, slightly angled optical paths, one per eye, which the brain combines into a three-dimensional view.

questions.q: How is magnification best defined?
o: The ability to distinguish two close points as separate, which actually describes resolution
The refractive index of the mounting medium, a property of the specimen preparation itself
The apparent increase in the size of an object, dependent on the focal length of the lenses used
The distance between the objective and the specimen, which actually describes working distance
questions.e: Magnification is the apparent increase in an object's size, and it depends on the focal length of the lenses in the optical system.

questions.q: How is resolution (resolving power) best defined?
o: The apparent size increase produced by a lens, which actually describes magnification
The brightness of the light source, a property controlled by the diaphragm and lamp
The working distance of the objective, the gap between its tip and the specimen
The ability to distinguish two points that are very close together as two separate entities
questions.e: Resolution is the ability of an optical system to tell apart two closely spaced points as two distinct points, rather than a single blur.

questions.q: What magnification range can an ordinary glass compound microscope typically achieve?
questions.e: An ordinary glass compound microscope typically spans a magnification range of about 25x to 1500x.

questions.q: What is the maximum useful magnification generally achievable with an oil-immersion compound light microscope?
questions.e: Oil-immersion compound microscopes can achieve up to about 2000x of genuinely useful magnification.

questions.q: What term describes magnifying an image beyond the point where any new detail becomes visible?
questions.e: "Empty magnification" is magnification beyond the resolution limit (roughly beyond 2000x for light microscopy) — the image gets bigger but no sharper.

questions.q: According to the theoretical maximal resolving power formula r = λ/2, what determines the absolute best resolution possible?
o: The magnification setting of the eyepiece
The thickness of the glass slide
The rotation speed of the nosepiece
The wavelength of the light used
questions.e: r = λ/2 shows that the best possible resolving power is set purely by the wavelength of light used — shorter wavelengths give finer theoretical resolution.

questions.q: Which wavelength of light is generally used as the reference point for microscope resolution because the human eye is most sensitive to it?
questions.e: Green light (λ ≈ 560 nm, often approximated as 600 nm) is used as the reference wavelength because the human eye is most sensitive to it.

questions.q: Two organelles are so close together that even at 2000x they still appear as a single blurred blob. What does this indicate?
o: The microscope's magnification is too low and should simply be increased further past the 2000x limit that has already been reached
The distance between the organelles is smaller than the microscope's resolving power, so higher magnification alone will not separate them
The eyepiece needs to be replaced with immersion oil, which actually coats the objective lens rather than the eyepiece itself
The organelles are moving too fast to be resolved by the optics, rather than simply sitting too close together to be separated
questions.e: If two points remain a single blur even at high magnification, their separation is below the resolution limit — pushing magnification higher only produces empty magnification, not separation.

questions.q: What does the formula NA = n sin U describe?
o: The total magnification of a compound microscope
The theoretical resolving power limit only
The numerical aperture of an objective lens
The working distance of an objective
questions.e: NA = n sin U is the formula for numerical aperture, combining the refractive index of the medium (n) and half the angular aperture (U).

questions.q: In the formula NA = n sin U, what does 'n' represent?
o: The number of lens elements in the objective, a design detail unrelated to this formula
The magnification power of the eyepiece, which does not appear in this formula at all
The number of wavelengths of light used, rather than a property of the medium itself
The refractive index of the medium between the objective lens and the specimen
questions.e: 'n' is the refractive index of the medium (air, water, glycerin or oil) between the objective lens and the specimen.

questions.q: In the formula NA = n sin U, what does 'U' represent?
o: Half of the angular aperture — half the angle of the cone of light entering the objective
The ultraviolet wavelength constant, a quantity that plays no part in this formula
The units of measurement being used, rather than an actual angle or optical quantity
The refractive index of the immersion oil, which is instead represented by 'n'
questions.e: 'U' is half the angular aperture, i.e. half the angle of the cone of light rays entering the objective lens from the specimen.

questions.q: What does the formula R = 0.61λ / NA calculate?
o: The total magnification of the microscope
The minimum resolvable distance between two points
The refractive index of immersion oil
The working distance of the condenser
questions.e: R = 0.61λ / NA gives the resolving power — the minimum distance between two points that the microscope can still show as separate.

questions.q: According to R = 0.61λ / NA, what happens to R (and therefore resolution) if NA increases while λ stays constant?
questions.e: Since NA is in the denominator, a larger NA produces a smaller R, meaning finer (better) resolution.

questions.q: According to R = 0.61λ / NA, what happens to resolution if a shorter wavelength (λ) of light is used, with NA constant?
o: Resolution gets worse, the opposite of what actually happens with a shorter wavelength
Resolution stays exactly the same, as if wavelength played no part in the formula
The formula no longer applies once the wavelength of light is changed at all
Resolution improves, because R decreases as the wavelength in the numerator shrinks
questions.e: A smaller λ in the numerator reduces R, meaning the microscope can resolve finer detail — this is why shorter wavelengths improve resolution.

questions.q: What is the refractive index of water?
questions.e: Water has a refractive index of about 1.33.

questions.q: What is the refractive index of immersion oil?
questions.e: Immersion oil has a refractive index of about 1.51 — the highest of the four media, closely matching glass.

questions.q: Why does using immersion oil instead of air between the objective and specimen improve resolution?
o: Oil lowers the refractive index, decreasing NA and thereby worsening resolution
Oil changes the wavelength of the light passing through it as it travels to the lens
Oil increases the working distance of the objective rather than its numerical aperture
Oil raises the refractive index, which increases NA and therefore decreases R, improving resolution
questions.e: Because NA = n sin U, the higher refractive index of oil (about 1.51) versus air (1.00) increases NA, which in turn decreases R in R = 0.61λ/NA, sharpening resolution.

questions.q: What is the approximate numerical aperture of a 40x oil-immersion Plan Fluorite objective?
questions.e: A 40x oil-immersion Plan Fluorite objective has an approximate NA of 1.30, much higher than the same objective used dry.

questions.q: Why do NA values generally increase from Plan Achromat, to Plan Fluorite, to Plan Apochromat objectives at the same magnification?
o: Apochromats use a completely different type of light source than achromats or fluorites do, which is not actually how these objectives work
Achromats are always used with lower-refractive-index oils than fluorite objectives, a claim not actually borne out by real design practice
Apochromat and fluorite objectives are built with more sophisticated lens correction, allowing them to accept a wider cone of light at a higher NA
NA has no relationship to objective design, only to magnification, which directly contradicts how numerical aperture is actually defined
questions.e: Fluorite and apochromat objectives use more advanced multi-element correction for spherical and chromatic aberration, which allows a wider, higher-NA cone of light to be captured and focused sharply, compared to a simpler achromat.

questions.q: A microscopist wants the best possible resolution. Which combination of choices would help the most, based on R = 0.61λ/NA and NA = n sin U?
o: Use a longer wavelength of light and a low-NA achromat objective in air
Use any wavelength, since NA has no effect on resolution according to this pairing
Increase the eyepiece magnification while keeping NA and λ the same throughout
Use a shorter wavelength of light and a high-NA apochromat objective with immersion oil
questions.e: Resolution improves when λ is minimised and NA is maximised (via a well-corrected high-NA objective and a high-refractive-index medium like immersion oil) — increasing eyepiece magnification alone does not improve resolution.

sets.name: Quiz 2 · Light Microscopy Techniques & Electron Microscopy

questions.q: In brightfield microscopy, how does the specimen typically appear?
questions.e: Brightfield is the standard technique: the specimen appears dark against a bright background, formed by light shaped into a cone by the substage condenser.

questions.q: Why do most unstained, transparent biological specimens need staining before brightfield viewing?
o: Staining increases the accelerating voltage, a concept that actually applies to electron beams, not light
Unstained transparent specimens produce very little contrast against the bright background
Staining sharpens the electromagnetic lenses, components that actually belong to electron microscopes
Staining freezes the tissue for cutting, a step that is actually done by physical fixation instead
questions.e: Brightfield relies on absorption to create contrast; transparent, colourless specimens barely absorb light, so staining is needed to make structures visible.

questions.q: Which structure shapes light from the illumination source into a cone focused at the specimen plane in brightfield microscopy?
questions.e: The substage condenser gathers and shapes the light into a cone that is focused precisely at the plane of the specimen.

questions.q: In darkfield microscopy, what blocks the direct light path so only scattered light reaches the specimen?
o: A dichroic mirror, a component that actually separates wavelengths in fluorescence microscopy
A fluorochrome filter, a component used in fluorescence microscopy rather than darkfield
A quartz lens in the objective, a component associated with ultraviolet microscopy instead
An opaque disc in the condenser that blocks the central beam of light entirely
questions.e: An opaque disc placed in the condenser blocks direct light, so the specimen is illuminated only by light scattered at an angle.

questions.q: How does the specimen appear under darkfield microscopy?
questions.e: Because only scattered light reaches the specimen, it appears bright and illuminated against a dark background — the opposite of brightfield.

questions.q: Darkfield microscopy is especially useful for viewing which kind of specimens?
o: Thick, opaque metal fragments, specimens that are instead examined well by an SEM
Unstained, live or transparent specimens such as spirochaete bacteria or yeast in liquid
Only specimens embedded in epoxy resin, a preparation step used for electron microscopy
Only specimens sectioned at 50-100 nm, the thin sections required for a TEM instead
questions.e: Darkfield is well suited to unstained, live or transparent specimens that are hard to see in brightfield, such as spirochaete bacteria or yeast cells in liquid.

questions.q: A researcher wants to visualise 40 nm gold particles. Which light-microscopy technique can detect such sub-diffraction particles?
questions.e: Darkfield can detect particles well below the normal diffraction limit, such as 40 nm gold particles, because their scattered light stands out against the dark background.

questions.q: What property of a transparent specimen does phase-contrast microscopy exploit to create contrast?
o: Differences in refractive index within the specimen
questions.e: Phase-contrast exploits small differences in refractive index within an otherwise transparent specimen, without needing any staining.

questions.q: What does phase-contrast microscopy convert into visible brightness/darkness differences?
o: Phase shifts in light passing through regions of the specimen with different refractive index
Differences in atomic mass, a property that instead governs contrast in electron microscopy
Differences in emitted fluorescence wavelength, a property relevant to fluorescence microscopy
Differences in accelerating voltage of the beam, a setting that applies to electron microscopes
questions.e: Light passing through denser regions is slightly shifted in phase; the phase-contrast optics convert this invisible phase shift into visible brightness differences.

questions.q: Which two optical components work together to produce the phase-contrast effect?
o: A dichroic mirror and a fluorochrome filter, components used in fluorescence microscopy instead
An annulus below the stage and a phase plate fitted in the objective lens itself
A diamond knife and a copper grid, tools used for electron microscopy sectioning instead
A quartz lens and an opaque condenser disc, components from UV and darkfield microscopy
questions.e: A special annulus below the stage shapes the illumination into a hollow cone, and a matching phase plate in the objective converts the resulting phase shifts into visible contrast.

questions.q: Phase-contrast microscopy is especially useful for observing which of the following?
o: Fractured metal components at high magnification, specimens better suited to an SEM
Ultra-thin resin sections under vacuum, a preparation used for electron microscopy instead
Live, unstained cells and internal structures such as nuclei and cytoplasmic flow
Specimens coated with heavy metals for electron density, a step used for EM instead
questions.e: Because it requires no staining, phase-contrast is ideal for observing live, unstained cells, including cell movement, nuclei and cytoplasmic flow.

questions.q: Phase-contrast observation of live cellular processes is often combined with which technique?
questions.e: Phase-contrast is often combined with time-lapse photography to record dynamic processes such as cell movement or cytoplasmic flow over time.

questions.q: Why does UV microscopy improve resolution compared with visible-light microscopy?
o: UV light has a shorter wavelength than visible light, roughly doubling resolution
UV light has a longer wavelength than visible light, which would actually worsen resolution
UV light passes through ordinary glass more easily, though in reality it does not
UV light does not need a condenser, though in reality UV optics still require one
questions.e: UV light has a shorter wavelength than visible light, and shorter wavelengths improve resolution — UV microscopy improves resolution roughly two-fold.

questions.q: Why do UV microscopes require special quartz lenses instead of ordinary glass optics?
o: Quartz is cheaper than glass, though in reality quartz optics cost considerably more
Glass absorbs UV light, so it cannot be used for UV-transparent optical components
Quartz produces fluorescence on its own, which is not the actual reason for its use
Glass lenses cannot focus visible light, though in reality glass focuses it perfectly well
questions.e: UV light cannot pass through glass, so UV microscopes need special, UV-transparent quartz lenses, which are expensive.

questions.q: Why can a UV microscope image not simply be viewed by eye through an eyepiece?
o: Because UV light has too long a wavelength to focus
Because UV requires a vacuum like electron microscopy
Because UV light is invisible to the human eye and can damage it
Because UV light cannot pass through the specimen at all
questions.e: UV light is invisible to the eye and can damage it, so UV images must be captured by a camera or projected onto a fluorescent screen instead.

questions.q: What happens when a fluorochrome such as fluorescein absorbs UV or shorter-wavelength light?
o: It is destroyed and produces no signal, rather than emitting light of its own
It reflects the light at exactly the same wavelength, unlike true fluorescent emission
It becomes electron-dense for TEM imaging, a property relevant to electron staining instead
It re-emits light at a longer, visible wavelength — the phenomenon called fluorescence
questions.e: Fluorescence is the absorption of shorter-wavelength light followed by near-instantaneous re-emission at a longer, visible wavelength.

questions.q: What is immunofluorescence?
o: Using antibodies chemically linked to fluorescein to visualise specific cellular proteins
Staining cytoplasm with eosin for routine histology, a technique unrelated to fluorescence
Freezing tissue in liquid nitrogen to prevent ice-crystal damage during fixation
Embedding tissue in epoxy resin for ultra-thin sectioning ahead of electron microscopy
questions.e: Immunofluorescence uses antibodies chemically linked to a fluorochrome like fluorescein to specifically label and visualise particular cellular proteins.

questions.q: In epifluorescence microscopy, what separates the excitation light from the emitted light?
o: A phase plate in the objective, a component that actually belongs to phase-contrast optics
A dichroic mirror that reflects excitation light while passing the longer emitted wavelength
An opaque disc in the condenser, a component that actually belongs to darkfield microscopy
A diamond knife, a tool that actually belongs to ultrathin sectioning for electron microscopy
questions.e: In epifluorescence, excitation and emission light both pass through the objective; a dichroic mirror separates the two based on wavelength.

questions.q: In epifluorescence microscopy, which lens do both the excitation light and the emitted light travel through?
o: Two separate condensers, one for excitation and one for the emitted fluorescence light
Two separate quartz lenses, one for excitation and one for the emitted fluorescence light
The same objective lens, used for both the excitation and the emitted light paths
No lens at all; only the fluorescent screen is used to capture the final image
questions.e: Epifluorescence is defined by excitation and emission light both travelling through the same objective, separated afterward by a dichroic mirror.

questions.q: What wave-like property of electrons underlies the potential for much higher resolution in electron microscopy?
o: Electrons carry no charge in a vacuum, a claim that is not actually true of electrons
Electrons always travel at the speed of light regardless of voltage, which is not the case
Electrons cannot be focused by magnetic fields, though in reality magnetic lenses focus them
Electrons have a wavelength that depends on accelerating voltage, lambda = sqrt 1.5/V nm
questions.e: Electrons have wave-like properties, with wavelength given by lambda = sqrt(1.5/V) nm, which shrinks as accelerating voltage V increases.

questions.q: Using lambda = sqrt(1.5/V) nm, roughly what electron wavelength is achieved at an accelerating voltage of 60 kV?
questions.e: At 60 kV the electron wavelength is approximately 0.005 nm, theoretically offering a huge resolution increase over visible light.

questions.q: In a TEM, what is the source of the electron beam?
questions.e: The TEM electron beam is emitted from a pin-shaped cathode and accelerated toward the specimen.

questions.q: What is the typical accelerating voltage range used in a TEM?
questions.e: TEMs typically operate with accelerating voltages of about 50-150 kV to drive electrons through the ultrathin specimen section.

questions.q: Why do biological specimens naturally produce weak contrast in a TEM?
o: They are always coated in fluorescein, a stain actually used for fluorescence microscopy
They are too thick to fit under the beam, which is not the actual reason for weak contrast
They absorb rather than scatter electrons completely, which does not match how tissue behaves
They are composed mainly of low atomic number elements such as carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen and oxygen
questions.e: Electron deflection depends on electron density/atomic mass; biological tissue is made mostly of low atomic number elements (C, H, N, O), giving inherently weak contrast without staining.

questions.q: What is the modern resolution achievable with a TEM?
questions.e: Modern TEMs can resolve about 0.2-0.3 nm, with useful magnification up to roughly 300,000 times.

questions.q: Where is the final image formed in a TEM?
o: Directly on the copper grid, the support that actually just holds the thin section
On a fluorescent screen or photographic/digital recording material below the specimen
On the glass slide used for light microscopy, which a TEM does not actually use
On the surface of the raw carrot support, a medium used only for cutting soft tissue
questions.e: The transmitted electron beam forms an image on a fluorescent screen or is recorded on photographic/digital material.

questions.q: Which condition is required for a TEM to operate, beyond staining and thin sectioning?
o: Bright ambient room lighting, which is not actually a requirement for TEM operation
Immersion in liquid nitrogen throughout imaging, which TEM operation does not require
A high vacuum, so that electrons are not scattered by air before reaching the specimen
A dichroic mirror, a component that actually belongs to fluorescence microscopy instead
questions.e: TEM requires a vacuum, because electrons would be scattered by air molecules before reaching the specimen and detector.

questions.q: What does an SEM image primarily reveal about a specimen?
o: Internal organelle ultrastructure via transmitted electrons
The refractive index differences within the cytoplasm
The fluorescence emission of labelled proteins
The surface topography of a solid specimen
questions.e: SEM uses electrons to image the surface of a solid specimen rather than transmitting electrons through a thin section.

questions.q: Why do SEM images have such an attractive, 3-D appearance?
o: Because of a large depth of field
Because specimens are stained with eosin
Because the sample is viewed underwater
Because SEM uses only visible light
questions.e: SEM's large depth of field is what produces the characteristic 3-D, textured look of its images.

questions.q: What is the typical resolution of a standard SEM (without a field-emission source)?
questions.e: Standard SEM resolution is around 10 nm, finer with a field-emission SEM (FESEM).

questions.q: Roughly what magnification range can a modern SEM reach, compared with light microscopy's ~2,000 times?
questions.e: SEM magnification can reach roughly 100,000-300,000 times, dramatically more than the ~2,000 times ceiling of light microscopy.

questions.q: Which of the following is a realistic use of SEM outside routine biology?
o: Observing live cell movement in real time, which SEM's vacuum chamber does not allow
Performing immunofluorescence labelling, a technique associated with light microscopy instead
Measuring refractive index of live cytoplasm, a task unrelated to how an SEM forms images
Examining fractured metal components, foreign particles, polymers and electronic components
questions.e: SEM is widely used in materials science too, for surfaces like fractured metal components, foreign particles, polymers and electronic components, as well as biological samples.

questions.q: What wavelength range of visible light does a light microscope use, giving it colour vision of the specimen?
questions.e: Light microscopes use visible light, roughly 390-760 nm, which is why the specimen can be seen in colour, unlike the monochrome image from electrons.

questions.q: Roughly what equivalent wavelength do the electrons used in electron microscopy have, and what does this mean for the image?
o: About 760 nm, giving a full colour image
About 4 nm, giving a monochrome image
About 0.2 nm, giving a colour image
About 4 micrometres, giving a monochrome image
questions.e: Electrons used in EM have an equivalent wavelength of roughly 4 nm, and since electrons carry no colour information, the resulting image is monochrome.

questions.q: Comparing maximum resolving power, which pairing is correct?
o: Light microscope ~0.2 nm, electron microscope ~240 nm
Both achieve about 10 nm resolving power
Light microscope ~240 nm, electron microscope ~0.2 nm
Light microscope ~4 nm, electron microscope ~760 nm
questions.e: A light microscope's maximum resolving power is about 240 nm, while an electron microscope can resolve down to about 0.2 nm.

questions.q: Comparing maximum magnification, which pairing is correct?
o: Light microscope x300,000-500,000; electron microscope x1,000-1,500, figures that are swapped
Both max out around x2,000, understating the true magnification range of an electron microscope
Light microscope x50-150; electron microscope x1,000-1,500, figures well below the real ranges
Light microscope x1,000-1,500; electron microscope x300,000-500,000, the correct pairing
questions.e: A light microscope typically maxes out around x1,000-1,500, while an electron microscope can reach x300,000-500,000.

questions.q: How do the radiation source and lens type compare between light and electron microscopes?
o: Light: tungsten/quartz-halogen lamp and glass lenses; Electron: high-voltage tungsten filament and magnetic/electromagnetic coil lenses
Light: high-voltage tungsten filament and magnetic lenses; Electron: quartz-halogen lamp and glass lenses, figures that are swapped around
Both use identical tungsten lamps and glass lenses, which ignores how differently each instrument is actually built
Light: magnetic coil lenses only; Electron: glass lenses only, a pairing that swaps the two lens types entirely
questions.e: Light microscopes use a tungsten or quartz-halogen lamp with glass lenses, whereas electron microscopes use a high-voltage tungsten filament with magnets/electromagnetic coils as lenses.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of fixation in specimen preparation?
o: To magnify the specimen before sectioning, a step actually performed by the microscope itself
To rapidly kill and preserve tissue, preventing autolysis and decay before further processing
To stain the nucleus blue for viewing, a step that actually happens later during staining
To create a vacuum around the specimen, a condition actually required only for electron microscopy
questions.e: Fixation rapidly kills and preserves tissue, preventing autolysis, bacterial/fungal attack, and damage from later procedures — it is fundamental to all histological work.

questions.q: In physical fixation, at what approximate temperature is liquid nitrogen used to rapidly freeze a specimen?
questions.e: Liquid nitrogen, an inert cryogenic fluid, freezes tissue at about -196 degrees C (-320 degrees F), fast enough to prevent ice-crystal formation.

questions.q: Why must physical fixation with liquid nitrogen be rapid?
o: To reduce the cost of quartz lenses, which freezing has no actual bearing on at all
To allow eosin to bind the cytoplasm, a staining step unrelated to the freezing process
To avoid needing a copper grid later, a support used only for electron microscopy sections
To prevent ice-crystal formation that would otherwise distort and damage the tissue
questions.e: Rapid freezing is essential to prevent the formation of ice crystals, which would otherwise physically distort and damage cellular structure.

questions.q: What is a key limitation of physical (freezing) fixation on its own?
o: Frozen tissue stays fixed only while frozen, so chemical fixation is still needed for permanence
It destroys all nucleic acids immediately, which freezing does not actually do to tissue
It cannot be performed at any temperature below 0 degrees C, though freezing requires exactly that
It works only for electron microscopy specimens, though freezing is also used for light microscopy
questions.e: Frozen tissue remains fixed only as long as it stays frozen; a permanent preparation still requires chemical fixation.

questions.q: What do chemical fixatives primarily stabilise within the cell?
o: Only carbohydrates, a class of molecules that fixatives do not specifically target
Proteins and lipids, the major structural components of the cell that fixatives stabilise
Only pigments visible in brightfield, which fixation does not specifically act upon
Only the electron beam path, a concept unrelated to how chemical fixatives actually work
questions.e: Chemical fixatives act by stabilising proteins and lipids, the two major structural components of cells and tissues.

questions.q: Which pair of fixatives is commonly used specifically to fix lipids for electron microscopy?
o: Formaldehyde and glutaraldehyde, the pair that instead fixes proteins for electron microscopy
Haematoxylin and eosin, a staining pair used in routine light microscopy, not lipid fixation
Osmium tetroxide and potassium permanganate, used specifically to fix lipids for EM
Acetic acid and mercuric chloride, a combination not used for lipid fixation in EM
questions.e: Osmium tetroxide and potassium permanganate are used to fix lipids for EM, while formaldehyde and glutaraldehyde are used to fix proteins.

questions.q: Why must water be removed from a specimen before it can be examined in an electron microscope?
o: Because water dissolves fluorochromes, which is not the reason water must be removed for EM
Because water prevents heavy metals from binding, which is not the actual reason for dehydration
Because water blocks visible light transmission, a concern that applies to light microscopy instead
Because electron microscopy requires a high vacuum that residual water would disrupt
questions.e: EM requires a high vacuum; water in the specimen would vaporise and disrupt the vacuum, so it must be dehydrated first.

questions.q: How is a specimen typically dehydrated before embedding?
o: Through a series of ethanol-water mixtures of increasing concentration up to 100% alcohol
By immersing it directly in molten paraffin wax, a step that actually comes after dehydration
By exposing it to UV light for several hours, a step unrelated to removing water from tissue
By coating it with uranium and lead, a step that instead happens during EM staining
questions.e: Dehydration is usually achieved with a graded series of ethanol-water mixtures, increasing in concentration up to 100% alcohol.

questions.q: After dehydration in alcohol, what reagent is commonly used to clear the specimen before wax infiltration, since alcohol and wax do not mix directly?
questions.e: A wax solvent such as xylene replaces the alcohol, bridging the gap between the dehydrating alcohol and the final wax (or resin) infiltration.

questions.q: For electron microscopy, what typically replaces the alcohol/xylene sequence before resin infiltration?
o: Liquid nitrogen at -196 degrees C, a step used for freezing rather than resin infiltration
Haematoxylin and eosin, a staining pair used in light microscopy, not resin infiltration
A resin solvent such as propylene oxide, bridging dehydration and resin infiltration
A copper grid, a support used to hold sections during electron microscopy, not infiltration
questions.e: For EM, dehydration continues with a resin solvent, propylene oxide, before the tissue is infiltrated with resin such as epoxy resin.

questions.q: Which embedding medium is used to support ultra-thin sections for electron microscopy?
questions.e: Epoxy resin, such as araldite, is hard enough to support the ultra-thin (~50 nm) sections required for electron microscopy.

questions.q: A plant specimen is too soft to cut cleanly for a thicker light-microscopy section. What temporary support medium can be used?
o: Raw carrot or pawpaw, firm plant tissue used to temporarily support soft specimens
Molten epoxy resin baked in an oven, a step used for permanent embedding, not temporary support
Liquid nitrogen at -196 degrees C, a step used for freezing rather than temporary support
A copper grid, a support used to hold ultrathin sections for electron microscopy instead
questions.e: Raw carrot or pawpaw can be used to temporarily support soft plant material while cutting thicker sections.

questions.q: What instrument is used to cut thin sections of embedded tissue?
o: A dichroic mirror, a component that actually belongs to fluorescence microscopy instead
A microtome, fitted with a specimen holder, cutting edge and thickness-control mechanism
A condenser, the lens beneath the stage that focuses light onto the specimen instead
A fluorescent screen, the surface that instead captures the image formed in a TEM
questions.e: A microtome — with a specimen holder, a sharp cutting edge, and a thickness-regulating mechanism — is used to section embedded tissue.

questions.q: Which cutting edge is typically used for wax-embedded specimens versus araldite-embedded specimens?
o: Diamond knife for wax; steel razor for araldite
Copper grid for wax; steel razor for araldite
Steel razor for wax; glass or diamond knife for araldite
Glass knife for wax; steel razor for araldite
questions.e: A steel razor is used for wax-embedded (light microscopy) specimens, while a glass or diamond knife is used for araldite-embedded (EM) specimens.

questions.q: Roughly what section thickness range is typical for light microscopy sections, compared with EM sections?
questions.e: Light microscopy sections are thicker, about 1,000-20,000 nm, while EM requires ultra-thin sections of about 50-100 nm.

questions.q: At what approximate temperature are frozen specimens cut on a microtome housed in a freezer?
questions.e: Frozen specimens are cut with a microtome in a freezer at around -20 degrees C, well above liquid nitrogen temperature but still frozen.

questions.q: Basic stains such as haematoxylin are positively charged (cationic). What do they primarily bind to?
o: Negatively charged molecules such as nucleic acids
Heavy metals like lead and uranium
questions.e: Basic (cationic) stains are positively charged and bind negatively charged molecules, such as nucleic acids, which is why haematoxylin stains the nucleus.

questions.q: Eosin is classified as which type of stain, and what does it typically colour?
o: A basic stain that colours the nucleus blue/purple
A negative EM stain that surrounds viruses
An acidic stain that colours the cytoplasm red
A fluorochrome that emits green light
questions.e: Eosin is an acidic (anionic) stain that binds basic groups in the cytoplasm, staining it red, complementing haematoxylin's nuclear staining.

questions.q: Which of the following is the classic, routine combined stain used for animal tissue histology?
questions.e: Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) together are the classic routine stain: haematoxylin marks the nucleus and eosin marks the cytoplasm.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of an acidic stain, rather than a basic stain?
questions.e: Picric acid is an acidic (anionic) stain, along with eosin, Nigrosine, Acid fuchsin and India ink; Crystal Violet, Methylene Blue and Safranin are basic stains.

questions.q: Why must EM stains contain heavy elements such as lead and uranium rather than coloured dyes?
o: Because heavy metals are cheaper than organic dyes, which is not the actual reason for their use
Because the image depends on an electron beam, so contrast must come from electron density, not colour
Because heavy metals fluoresce under UV light, which is not why they are used in EM staining
Because light microscopy stains dissolve resin, which is not the reason EM avoids coloured dyes
questions.e: Since EM images are formed by an electron beam, stains must increase electron density to create contrast — colour is irrelevant to the electron image.

questions.q: In positive EM staining, how does the heavy-metal stain interact with the specimen?
o: It surrounds the specimen without binding it, the pattern seen instead in negative staining
It only labels fluorescent antibodies, a description that belongs to immunofluorescence instead
It binds directly to structures such as membranes and ribosomes, increasing their electron density
It dissolves the structure entirely, which positive staining does not actually do to tissue
questions.e: In positive staining, heavy-metal stains bind directly to structures — used for isolated organelles, membranes, viruses and ribosomes.

questions.q: What is the EM equivalent of the H&E staining technique used in light microscopy?
o: The negative staining technique with phosphotungstate, used for viruses and isolated particles
The osmium tetroxide fixation step alone, which fixes lipids rather than providing routine contrast
The basic fuchsin stain, a light-microscopy dye not actually used as an EM equivalent of H&E
The uranium and lead double-stain technique used routinely to provide contrast in EM sections
questions.e: The uranium + lead double-stain technique is considered the EM equivalent of H&E, providing routine positive-stain contrast for EM sections.

questions.q: What is the smallest unit of life capable of independently performing all the functions of life?
questions.e: The cell is the smallest unit of life that can independently carry out functions such as growth, reproduction, and metabolism.

questions.q: The cell is described as the basic structural and functional unit of which of the following?
questions.e: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms, from bacteria to humans.

questions.q: According to Cell Theory, all living things are composed of what?
questions.e: The first tenet of Cell Theory states that all living things are composed of one or more cells.

questions.q: According to Cell Theory, the cell is the basic unit of what in organisms?
questions.e: The second tenet states that the cell is the basic unit of structure and organization in organisms.

questions.q: According to Cell Theory, new cells arise from what?
o: Only from nuclei separated from a parent
questions.e: The third tenet of Cell Theory states that cells arise only from pre-existing cells, through the process of cell division.

questions.q: How many core tenets make up the classical statement of Cell Theory covered in this module?
questions.e: Cell Theory is built on three tenets: all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of organization, and cells arise from pre-existing cells.

questions.q: Which statement correctly reflects Cell Theory's view on the origin of new cells?
o: Cells can arise spontaneously from non-living material
Cells arise only inside the nucleus
Cells only arise from the division of pre-existing cells
questions.e: Cell Theory rejects spontaneous generation — new cells arise only from pre-existing cells dividing.

questions.q: A single bacterium, though unicellular, is still considered fully alive because it exhibits which property?
o: It has a nucleus, a feature that bacteria as prokaryotes actually lack
It has membrane-bound organelles, structures that bacteria as prokaryotes lack
It is larger than eukaryotic cells, though bacteria are actually much smaller
It exhibits all major properties of life despite being one cell
questions.e: Even simple unicellular organisms exhibit all major properties of life — growth, reproduction, response to stimuli, and metabolism.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three tenets of Cell Theory?
o: All cells must have a nucleus, though prokaryotic cells clearly lack one
All living things are composed of one or more cells
The cell is the basic unit of structure and organization
Cells arise only from pre-existing cells, through cell division
questions.e: Cell Theory does not require a nucleus — prokaryotic cells lack a nucleus yet are still cells, per the first two tenets.

questions.q: Why does Cell Theory reject the idea that cells can form spontaneously from non-living matter?
o: Because non-living matter cannot contain water
Because cells arise only from pre-existing cells via division
Because only eukaryotic cells can form
Because spontaneous generation only applies to viruses
questions.e: The third tenet of Cell Theory establishes that cells come only from the division of pre-existing cells, ruling out spontaneous generation.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the defining abilities shared by all living cells?
questions.e: Growth is one of the defining abilities of living cells, along with reproduction, processing information, responding to stimuli, and carrying out chemical reactions.

questions.q: Processing information and responding to stimuli are examples of what?
o: Abilities that define a living cell
questions.e: Processing information and responding to stimuli are among the defining abilities that living cells share, regardless of complexity.

questions.q: Carrying out chemical reactions that sustain life is best described as which property of cells?
questions.e: Carrying out the chemical reactions that sustain life is the cell's metabolic activity, one of the key defining abilities of life.

questions.q: Confining chemical reactions to specialized structures within a cell is known as what general cell function?
questions.e: Compartmentalization is the general cell function of confining chemical reactions within specialized structures inside the cell.

questions.q: Regulating the inflow and outflow of materials across the cell boundary is an example of which general cell function?
questions.e: Cells regulate the inflow and outflow of materials across their boundary as one of their general functions.

questions.q: What does a cell use to direct its own activities?
questions.e: A cell uses its genetic material (DNA) to direct and coordinate its activities.

questions.q: The idea that new cells and organisms arise only from existing cells reflects which general function of the cell?
questions.e: The continuity of life originates from the cell — new cells arise only from existing cells, ensuring life's continuity.

questions.q: Approximately how many cells are estimated to make up the human body?
questions.e: The human body is estimated to contain roughly 100 trillion cells.

questions.q: Approximately how many different cell types exist in the human body?
questions.e: The human body is organized into roughly 200 different cell types, such as neurons, muscle cells, and red blood cells.

questions.q: Why do cells across the human body vary so much in size and shape?
o: Random chance during development, with no relationship to cell function
All cells are actually the same size, which does not match observed variation
Only skin cells vary in shape, while every other cell type stays uniform
Variation is related to the specific function each cell type performs
questions.e: Cells vary in size and shape in ways that are closely related to the specific function each cell type performs.

questions.q: What are the two fundamental categories that every cell on Earth falls into?
questions.e: Every cell is classified as either prokaryotic (without a nucleus) or eukaryotic (with a nucleus).

questions.q: A prokaryotic cell is best defined as a cell that lacks what?
questions.e: A prokaryotic cell is defined by the lack of a membrane-bound nucleus, distinguishing it from eukaryotic cells.

questions.q: A eukaryotic cell is defined by the presence of what structure?
o: A cell wall in every case
questions.e: Eukaryotic cells are defined by having a true, membrane-bound nucleus that encloses their DNA.

questions.q: In a prokaryotic cell, where does the DNA lie?
o: Enclosed in a nuclear envelope, as in eukaryotic cells rather than prokaryotes
Inside mitochondria, organelles that prokaryotic cells do not actually possess
Wrapped around the cell wall, rather than lying free within the cell
Free in the cytoplasm, concentrated in the nucleoid region rather than enclosed in a nucleus
questions.e: Prokaryotic DNA lies free in the cytoplasm, concentrated in a region called the nucleoid, rather than being enclosed in a nuclear envelope.

questions.q: In prokaryotes, DNA is NOT wrapped around which type of protein, unlike in eukaryotes?
questions.e: Prokaryotic DNA is not wrapped around histones, the DNA-packaging proteins characteristic of eukaryotic cells.

questions.q: What chemical makes up the cell wall of Bacteria (a domain of prokaryotes)?
questions.e: Bacterial cell walls are made of peptidoglycan, a distinctive polymer of sugars and amino acids.

questions.q: How do Archaea (a domain of prokaryotes) cell walls differ from Bacterial cell walls?
o: Archaea have no cell wall at all, though most Archaea do possess one
Archaea walls are made of peptidoglycan too, which is actually a Bacterial trait
Archaea have tough walls made of other, distinct chemicals
Archaea walls are identical to eukaryotic cellulose walls, which is not the case
questions.e: Archaea have tough cell walls made of chemicals distinct from the peptidoglycan found in Bacteria.

questions.q: Which of the following is characteristic of prokaryotic internal structure?
o: A membrane-bound nucleus surrounded by organelles
questions.e: Prokaryotes lack complex, membrane-bound organelles, which is one of the three key axes distinguishing them from eukaryotes.

questions.q: Which three axes are used in this module to distinguish prokaryotes from eukaryotes?
o: DNA packaging, cell wall makeup, and internal structures
Color, shape, and mobility, none of which are the axes used in this module
Size, taste, and smell, none of which are actual distinguishing axes
Reproduction rate, diet, and habitat, none of which this module uses
questions.e: The three key distinguishing axes covered are DNA packaging, cell wall makeup, and internal (organelle) structures.

questions.q: Which of these organelles would you expect to find in a eukaryotic cell but NOT a prokaryotic cell?
o: Cytoplasm, a component actually present in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
Mitochondria, the membrane-bound organelles unique to eukaryotic cells
Plasma membrane, a structure actually present in both cell categories
Ribosomes are absent in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, so neither actually has them
questions.e: Mitochondria are membrane-bound organelles present in eukaryotic cells but absent from prokaryotic cells.

questions.q: Compared to eukaryotic cells, prokaryotic cells are generally what size?
o: Size is unrelated to cell type
questions.e: Prokaryotic cells generally have a smaller cell size than eukaryotic cells.

questions.q: Prokaryotic form and function is characterized by which kind of internal organization?
o: No internal organization of any kind
questions.e: Prokaryotic cells have a simpler internal organization than eukaryotic cells, lacking internal membrane-bound compartments.

questions.q: Which region in a prokaryotic cell holds its DNA in the absence of a nucleus?
questions.e: The nucleoid is the region of the prokaryotic cytoplasm where the free DNA is concentrated, since there is no nuclear envelope.

questions.q: Bacteria and Archaea are both examples of which broad cell category?
questions.e: Bacteria and Archaea are both domains of prokaryotic organisms, cells that lack a membrane-bound nucleus.

questions.q: Animals, plants, fungi, and protists are all examples of organisms built from which cell category?
questions.e: Animals, plants, fungi and protists are all eukaryotes — organisms whose cells possess a true, membrane-bound nucleus.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares DNA packaging in prokaryotes and eukaryotes?
o: Both wrap DNA around histones equally, though prokaryotes actually lack this
Neither prokaryotes nor eukaryotes have DNA, which is clearly not true
Eukaryotic DNA is never wrapped around anything, though histones actually do this
Prokaryotic DNA is not wrapped around histones; eukaryotic DNA is
questions.e: A key distinguishing feature is that prokaryotic DNA is not wrapped around histones, while eukaryotic DNA typically is.

questions.q: If a cell has a peptidoglycan cell wall, free cytoplasmic DNA, and no membrane-bound organelles, it is most likely which kind of cell?
questions.e: Peptidoglycan cell walls are characteristic specifically of Bacteria, a domain of prokaryotic cells, along with free cytoplasmic DNA and no membrane-bound organelles.

questions.q: If a cell has a tough cell wall made of chemicals other than peptidoglycan, plus free cytoplasmic DNA, which domain does it most likely belong to?
questions.e: Archaea are prokaryotes with tough cell walls made of chemicals distinct from the peptidoglycan found in Bacteria.

questions.q: Which feature is shared by BOTH prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
questions.e: Both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells use DNA as their genetic material — the difference lies in how and where that DNA is packaged and stored.

questions.q: A student observes a cell with a membrane-bound nucleus and multiple membrane-bound organelles. What category is this cell?
questions.e: A membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles are defining features of eukaryotic cells.

questions.q: Which single feature is the clearest defining difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
o: Presence or absence of a membrane-bound nucleus
questions.e: The presence or absence of a true, membrane-bound nucleus is the single clearest defining difference between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.

questions.q: Which of the following is listed as a factor that determines the shape of a cell?
o: The color of the cytoplasm, a property that does not shape a cell at all
The surface tension and viscosity of the cytoplasm
The number of ribosomes present, which does not determine a cell's shape
The temperature of the room only, which has no real effect on cell shape
questions.e: Cell shape is partly determined by the surface tension and viscosity of the cytoplasm.

questions.q: How can the mechanical action of adjoining cells affect a cell's shape?
o: It has no effect on shape, which does not match how tissue cells behave
It only affects prokaryotic cells, which typically lack neighboring cell contact
Pressure and contact from neighboring cells can reshape a cell
It changes the cell's genetic material, rather than its physical shape
questions.e: The mechanical action that adjoining cells exert on each other can flatten or reshape a cell, such as in tightly packed tissue.

questions.q: How does the rigidity of the cell membrane relate to cell shape?
o: Membrane rigidity has no bearing on shape
Only cell walls affect rigidity, never the membrane
Rigid membranes only occur in eukaryotes
A more rigid membrane holds a more fixed shape
questions.e: A more rigid cell membrane (or wall) tends to hold a more fixed shape, while a flexible membrane allows more variable shapes.

questions.q: A nerve cell's long, elongated shape is best explained by which factor determining cell shape?
questions.e: A cell's shape is often adapted to the specific function it performs — a nerve cell's elongated shape suits its role in transmitting signals over distance.

questions.q: For a cube-shaped cell with a side length of 1 cm, what is its total surface area?
questions.e: Surface area of a cube = 6 × side² = 6 × (1 cm)² = 6 cm².

questions.q: For a cube-shaped cell with a side length of 1 cm, what is its volume?
questions.e: Volume of a cube = side³ = (1 cm)³ = 1 cm³.

questions.q: For a cube-shaped cell with a side length of 1 cm, what is its surface-area-to-volume (SA:V) ratio?
questions.e: SA:V = surface area ÷ volume = 6 cm² ÷ 1 cm³ = 6 cm⁻¹.

questions.q: For a cube-shaped cell with a side length of 2 cm, what is its total surface area?
questions.e: Surface area of a cube = 6 × side² = 6 × (2 cm)² = 6 × 4 = 24 cm².

questions.q: For a cube-shaped cell with a side length of 2 cm, what is its volume?
questions.e: Volume of a cube = side³ = (2 cm)³ = 8 cm³.

questions.q: For a cube-shaped cell with a side length of 2 cm, what is its SA:V ratio?
questions.e: SA:V = 24 cm² ÷ 8 cm³ = 3 cm⁻¹.

questions.q: For a cube-shaped cell with a side length of 4 cm, what is its total surface area?
questions.e: Surface area of a cube = 6 × side² = 6 × (4 cm)² = 6 × 16 = 96 cm².

questions.q: For a cube-shaped cell with a side length of 4 cm, what is its volume?
questions.e: Volume of a cube = side³ = (4 cm)³ = 64 cm³.

questions.q: For a cube-shaped cell with a side length of 4 cm, what is its SA:V ratio?
questions.e: SA:V = 96 cm² ÷ 64 cm³ = 1.5 cm⁻¹.

questions.q: As a cube-shaped cell's side length doubles from 1 cm to 2 cm, how does its volume change?
questions.e: Volume scales with the cube of the side length, so doubling the side length (1 cm → 2 cm) increases volume from 1 cm³ to 8 cm³, an eightfold increase.

questions.q: As a cube-shaped cell's side length doubles from 1 cm to 2 cm, how does its surface area change?
questions.e: Surface area scales with the square of the side length, so doubling the side length increases surface area from 6 cm² to 24 cm², a fourfold increase.

questions.q: Why does the SA:V ratio fall as a cube-shaped cell grows larger?
o: Because volume grows cubically while surface area grows only squarely
Because surface area grows faster than volume, the opposite of what happens
Because both grow at exactly the same rate, which would keep SA:V constant
Because volume shrinks as cells grow, which is not what actually happens
questions.e: Volume increases with the cube of side length while surface area increases only with the square, so the SA:V ratio necessarily falls as size increases.

questions.q: Going from a 1 cm cube to a 4 cm cube, how does the SA:V ratio change?
o: It rises from 6 cm⁻¹ to 24 cm⁻¹
It falls from 6 cm⁻¹ to 1.5 cm⁻¹
It falls from 1.5 cm⁻¹ to 6 cm⁻¹
questions.e: The SA:V ratio falls from 6 cm⁻¹ (at 1 cm) to 1.5 cm⁻¹ (at 4 cm) as the cube grows, exactly as the worked table shows.

questions.q: Of the three cube sizes in the worked table (1 cm, 2 cm, 4 cm), which has the HIGHEST SA:V ratio, and therefore the most efficient diffusion relative to its volume?
o: The 4 cm cube, the largest of the three sizes in the worked table
The 2 cm cube, the middle of the three sizes in the worked table
The 1 cm cube, the smallest of the three sizes in the worked table
All three have exactly equal SA:V ratios, regardless of their differing cube sizes
questions.e: The smallest cube (1 cm side) has the highest SA:V ratio (6 cm⁻¹), giving it the most surface area relative to volume for efficient diffusion.

questions.q: Why do cells need a high surface-area-to-volume ratio?
o: To increase their genetic material, which SA:V ratio has no effect on
To reduce the number of organelles needed, which SA:V ratio does not govern
To make cell division impossible, the opposite of what a high SA:V supports
For efficient diffusion of nutrients, gases, and waste relative to metabolic demand
questions.e: A high SA:V ratio allows efficient diffusion of nutrients, gases and waste across the plasma membrane relative to the cell's metabolic demand, which scales with volume.

questions.q: What defining structural feature do all microbodies share?
o: A single limiting membrane, unlike double-membraned organelles
A double membrane like mitochondria, though microbodies actually have only one
No membrane at all, though microbodies are in fact membrane-bound
A membrane continuous with the nuclear envelope, unlike a true microbody
questions.e: Microbodies are usually oval/spherical and bounded by a single membrane, unlike double-membraned organelles such as mitochondria.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four organelle types grouped under 'microbodies'?
questions.e: Microbodies encompass peroxisomes, glyoxysomes, hydrogenosomes and glycosomes; lysosomes are a separate, distinct organelle formed via the Golgi.

questions.q: Urate oxidase converts urate into which products?
questions.e: Urate oxidase performs purine catabolism, converting urate into allantoin, CO₂ and H₂O₂.

questions.q: D-amino acids that peroxisomal D-amino acid oxidase acts on originate mainly from where?
o: The mitochondria, though D-amino acids do not actually originate there
The Golgi apparatus, though D-amino acids do not actually originate there
Photosynthesis in plant cells, an unrelated process for animal cells
Breakdown of proteins by gut bacteria, releasing toxic D-amino acids
questions.e: Gut bacteria break down proteins and release toxic D-amino acids, which D-amino acid oxidase then degrades to oxoacids plus H₂O₂.

questions.q: What is the role of catalase in a peroxisome?
o: It rapidly degrades H₂O₂ to water and O₂
questions.e: Catalase rapidly degrades the toxic oxidizing agent H₂O₂ produced by oxidase reactions, converting it to harmless water and oxygen.

questions.q: How do new peroxisomes typically form?
o: By budding directly from the nucleus
questions.e: Unlike lysosomes, which derive from the Golgi, peroxisomes form by division of pre-existing peroxisomes.

questions.q: Besides purine catabolism, what toxic substances do peroxisomes oxidize as part of normal metabolism?
o: Glucose and starch, molecules that peroxisomes do not oxidize this way
DNA and RNA, molecules that peroxisomes do not oxidize as toxins
Alcohol and formaldehyde, oxidized as part of normal peroxisomal metabolism
Cholesterol and bile salts, which are not oxidized in this pathway
questions.e: Peroxisomes participate in amino-acid and fatty-acid metabolism and also oxidize toxic substances such as alcohol and formaldehyde.

questions.q: Glyoxysomes are characterised by enzymes of which metabolic cycle?
questions.e: Glyoxysomes are plant-cell microbodies where enzymes of the glyoxylate cycle predominate, converting stored fats into transportable sugars.

questions.q: In glyoxysome metabolism, stored fats are first degraded to which intermediate?
questions.e: Fats degrade to acetyl CoA, which feeds the glyoxylate cycle to yield succinate, later used for gluconeogenesis in the mitochondria.

questions.q: After the glyoxylate cycle produces succinate, where is it transported and for what purpose?
o: To the nucleus, for a supposed role in DNA repair
To the mitochondria, as a substrate for gluconeogenesis
To the Golgi, for a supposed role in glycosylation
To the lysosome, for a supposed role in digestion
questions.e: Succinate is transported to the mitochondria, where it serves as a substrate for gluconeogenesis (sugar synthesis) to feed growing plant tissues.

questions.q: Hydrogenosomes are found in which type of organism, and are named for releasing what gas?
questions.e: Hydrogenosomes occur in anaerobic eukaryotic cells (ciliates, trichomonads, some fungi and animals) and are named for releasing molecular hydrogen (H₂) during anaerobic energy generation.

questions.q: In which vertebrate organs are microbodies particularly abundant?
questions.e: Microbodies are found in large numbers in the liver and kidneys of vertebrates, as well as in plant leaves/seeds and in protozoa, yeasts and fungi.

questions.q: Where are lysosomes formed within the cell?
questions.e: Lysosomes are membranous vesicles formed in the Golgi complex and filled with digestive enzymes.

questions.q: To what approximate internal pH do lysosomes pump H⁺ ions?
questions.e: Lysosomes pump in H⁺ ions until the internal pH reaches about 5.0, the pH at which their hydrolytic enzymes become active.

questions.q: Approximately how many distinct hydrolytic enzymes does a lysosome contain?
questions.e: A lysosome contains roughly 60 hydrolytic enzymes (hydrolases) that are active at acid pH.

questions.q: Digestion of foreign, extracellular material by a lysosome is called what?
questions.e: Heterophagy is the lysosomal digestion of foreign extracellular material, as opposed to autophagy, which recycles the cell's own organelles.

questions.q: A lysosome digesting a worn-out mitochondrion within its own cell is an example of what process?
questions.e: Autophagy is the intracellular recycling of a cell's own organelles, such as worn-out mitochondria or ribosomes, via the lysosome.

questions.q: What enzyme in the lysosomal membrane is responsible for acidifying the lysosomal interior?
questions.e: An H⁺-ATPase in the lysosomal membrane actively pumps protons into the lumen, producing the acidic pH (~5.0) that activates the hydrolases.

questions.q: From which part of the Golgi apparatus are the coated vesicles that become primary lysosomes released?
questions.e: Primary lysosomes derive from coated vesicles released from the trans cisternae of the Golgi apparatus.

questions.q: What forms when an endosome (from receptor-mediated endocytosis) fuses with a primary lysosome?
questions.e: Fusion of an endosome with a primary lysosome produces a secondary lysosome, which digests its contents.

questions.q: Why is the lysosomal membrane not digested by its own contents?
o: It is resistant to its own hydrolases and impermeable to enzymes/substrates
It lacks any enzymes inside it, though lysosomes are packed with hydrolases
It is constantly replaced every second, which is not actually how it survives
It has no membrane at all, though the lysosome is clearly membrane-bound
questions.e: The lysosomal membrane is resistant to its own hydrolases and impermeable to enzymes and substrates, though it is freely permeable to small digestion products.

questions.q: What ultimately kills phagocytes that have engulfed inhaled silica particles, leading to silicosis?
o: Silica particles block the nuclear pores, which is not the actual mechanism
The silica particles rupture the lysosomal membrane, releasing enzymes into the cytosol
Silica particles bind directly to DNA, which is not what causes phagocyte death
Silica particles dissolve the plasma membrane instantly, which is not the mechanism
questions.e: Silica particles rupture the lysosomal membrane inside phagocytes, releasing digestive enzymes that kill the cell and trigger fibrosis.

questions.q: What long-term tissue change results from repeated phagocyte death in silicosis?
o: Increased lung elasticity, the opposite of what silicosis actually causes
New alveoli regenerate rapidly, which does not occur in silicosis
Fibroblasts deposit collagen, reducing lung elasticity
The liver becomes enlarged, an organ that silicosis does not primarily affect
questions.e: Repeated phagocyte death from ruptured lysosomes triggers fibroblasts to deposit collagen, which reduces lung elasticity in silicosis.

questions.q: Asbestosis and black lung disease share the same underlying mechanism as silicosis but are caused by which particles respectively?
questions.e: Asbestosis is caused by inhaled asbestos fibres and black lung disease by coal dust, both rupturing lysosomes via the same mechanism as silicosis.

questions.q: The outer membrane of the nuclear envelope is continuous with which other structure?
questions.e: The outer membrane of the nuclear envelope is continuous with the rough endoplasmic reticulum.

questions.q: What space separates the inner and outer membranes of the nuclear envelope?
questions.e: The double membrane of the nuclear envelope is separated by the perinuclear space.

questions.q: Nuclear pores form where which structures fuse?
o: The inner and outer nuclear membranes
questions.e: Nuclear pores form at points where the outer and inner nuclear membranes fuse together.

questions.q: How many protein granules make up the 'annulus' surrounding a nuclear pore?
questions.e: Each nuclear pore is surrounded by an annulus of eight protein granules arranged symmetrically.

questions.q: What is the combined term for a nuclear pore plus its surrounding annulus?
