questions.e: The pore together with its annulus is called a porosome.

questions.q: How can proteins larger than the nuclear pore itself still enter the nucleus?
o: They cannot enter under any circumstances
Via a signal sequence enabling selective transport
By first being digested into smaller fragments
By diffusing passively regardless of size
questions.e: A signal sequence on a nuclear protein allows selective accumulation in the nucleus even for molecules larger than the pore.

questions.q: Approximately what fraction of a eukaryotic chromosome is DNA versus protein?
questions.e: Eukaryotic chromosomes are roughly one-third DNA and two-thirds protein.

questions.q: Chromatin is a nucleoprotein complex made of DNA plus which proteins?
questions.e: Chromatin is the nucleoprotein complex of small, basic proteins called histones, together with non-histone proteins.

questions.q: Chromatin is organised into repeating structural units called what?
questions.e: Chromatin is organised into repeating units called nucleosomes, made of DNA wrapped around histone proteins.

questions.q: How many chromosomes does a typical human somatic cell have?
questions.e: Humans have 46 chromosomes in their somatic cells.

questions.q: How does chromatin packing differ between non-dividing and dividing cells?
o: It is identical in both states, though packing clearly differs between them
Tightly packed in non-dividing cells, loose in dividing cells
Loosely packed in non-dividing cells, tightly packed in dividing cells
Chromatin disappears entirely during division, which is not what happens
questions.e: Non-dividing cells have loosely packed chromatin (for gene access), while dividing cells have tightly packed chromosomes after DNA doubles and condenses.

questions.q: In protein synthesis, DNA is transcribed into which molecule before translation occurs?
questions.e: DNA is transcribed into messenger RNA (mRNA), which is then translated into an amino-acid sequence to build a protein.

questions.q: How many centrioles make up a centrosome, and at what angle are they arranged?
questions.e: A centrosome is composed of 2 centrioles positioned at 90° to each other.

questions.q: Each centriole in a centrosome is built from how many microtubule triplets arranged in a ring?
questions.e: Each centriole contains 9 clusters of 3 microtubules (triplets) arranged in a ring.

questions.q: What region of the centrosome is the site of mitotic spindle and microtubule formation?
questions.e: The pericentriolar area of the centrosome is the site where the mitotic spindle and cytoplasmic microtubules form.

questions.q: At which end of a microtubule, relative to the centrosome, does rapid lengthening and shortening occur?
o: The minus end, closest to the centrosome, where growth is far slower
Both ends equally, though the two ends actually behave quite differently
Neither end — only the middle changes, which is not how microtubules grow
The plus end, farthest from the centrosome, where growth is fastest
questions.e: The 'plus' end of a microtubule, farthest from the centrosome, is where rapid lengthening and shortening takes place.

questions.q: Which cytoskeletal filament type has the largest diameter, at about 25 nm?
questions.e: Microtubules are the thickest of the three filament types, at roughly 25 nm in diameter, built from tubulin.

questions.q: Intermediate filaments, at about 10 nm in diameter, are built primarily from which protein family?
questions.e: Intermediate filaments (~10 nm) are built from keratin-family proteins and provide resistance to mechanical stress.

questions.q: Actin filaments (microfilaments), the thinnest of the three types at about 8 nm, are built from which protein?
questions.e: Actin filaments, roughly 8 nm in diameter, are polymers of the protein actin.

questions.q: Which two motor proteins are associated with microtubules?
questions.e: Kinesin and dynein are the motor ('mover') proteins associated with microtubules.

questions.q: Which motor protein is associated with actin filaments?
questions.e: Myosin is the motor protein associated with actin filaments, driving processes like muscle contraction and cytokinesis.

questions.q: Which filament type has no associated motor protein, but instead functions mainly to resist mechanical stress?
o: Microtubules, which actually do have an associated motor protein
Intermediate filaments, which lack a motor protein of their own
Actin filaments, which actually do have an associated motor protein
None — all three actually have their own motor proteins
questions.e: Intermediate filaments lack an associated motor protein; their main role is resisting mechanical stress rather than driving movement.

questions.q: Actin filaments are especially important in which three functional roles?
o: Axoneme movement, ribosome assembly, DNA repair
questions.e: Actin filaments function in membrane contraction, muscle cell contraction, and cytokinesis (cell division).

questions.q: Microtubules are especially important in which three functional roles?
o: Membrane contraction, muscle cells, cytokinesis, roles that belong elsewhere
Resisting mechanical stress only, a role that instead belongs to intermediate filaments
Fat storage and gluconeogenesis, roles unrelated to microtubule function
Cytoplasmic transport, axoneme movement, and chromosome movement during division
questions.e: Microtubules function in cytoplasmic transport, axoneme (cilia/flagella) movement, and chromosome movement during division.

questions.q: A microtubule's wall is formed from how many protofilaments arranged in parallel around a central lumen?
questions.e: 13 protofilaments, each built from polymerized tubulin dimers, arrange in parallel to form the circular microtubule wall around a central lumen.

questions.q: Which microtubule-associated protein (MAP) is implicated in Alzheimer's disease when it forms tangled filaments?
questions.e: Tau protein, a MAP that normally stabilizes microtubules, forms tangled filaments in Alzheimer's disease as microtubules are lost from axons.

questions.q: In Alzheimer's disease, what happens to microtubules in axons as tau tangles accumulate?
o: They become more numerous and stable
They are lost from axons, impairing axonal transport
They fuse into a single giant microtubule
questions.e: Microtubules are lost from axons in Alzheimer's disease, and impaired axonal transport contributes to nerve-cell dysfunction.

questions.q: Why is the mitotic spindle a useful target for anti-cancer drugs?
o: It is unrelated to cell division, though the spindle is central to mitosis
It only exists in cancer cells, though every dividing cell forms a spindle
It is located outside the cell, though the spindle forms within the cytoplasm
Its microtubule growth/shrinkage drives chromosome alignment and separation during division
questions.e: Because mitotic spindle microtubules must grow and shrink to align and separate chromosomes, disrupting them blocks the uncontrolled division characteristic of cancer.

questions.q: What are the two general anti-cancer drug strategies that target microtubules?
o: Disrupt microtubule assembly, or lock/stabilize assembled microtubules
Increase or decrease cell size, a strategy that does not target microtubules
Block DNA replication only, a mechanism unrelated to microtubule-targeting drugs
Destroy the nucleus, or destroy the Golgi, neither of which describes these drugs
questions.e: Anti-cancer agents either disrupt microtubule assembly (block polymerization) or lock/stabilize already-assembled microtubules — both halt mitosis.

questions.q: How does Taxol block cell division?
o: It prevents tubulin dimers from ever forming, which is not how Taxol works
It inhibits microtubule disassembly, locking microtubules static
It destroys the nuclear envelope, which is not Taxol's mechanism at all
It activates catalase to overproduce H₂O₂, unrelated to Taxol's actual mechanism
questions.e: Taxol inhibits microtubule disassembly, freezing microtubules in a static, locked state so the spindle cannot function.

questions.q: Colchicine, nocodazole and vincristine share which mechanism of action?
o: They stabilize and lock microtubules, like Taxol, which is the opposite mechanism
They repair damaged DNA, a mechanism unrelated to these three drugs
They inhibit microtubule assembly, blocking polymerisation and promoting depolymerisation
They increase lysosomal pH, a mechanism unrelated to how these three drugs work
questions.e: Colchicine, nocodazole and vincristine all inhibit microtubule assembly by blocking polymerisation and promoting depolymerisation.

questions.q: Which of these microtubule-assembly inhibitors is actually used clinically in cancer chemotherapy?
questions.e: Vincristine, which inhibits microtubule assembly, is used in clinical cancer chemotherapy regimens.

questions.q: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex, a blistering skin disease, results from a defect in which cytoskeletal component?
questions.e: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex results from a lack of normal keratin filament bundles, a type of intermediate filament, weakening skin cells against mechanical stress.

questions.q: Mallory bodies, seen in alcoholic liver cirrhosis, form from the accumulation of which protein?
questions.e: Alcoholic liver cirrhosis involves accumulation of keratin filaments in liver cells, forming aggregates known as Mallory bodies.

questions.q: Alzheimer's disease is linked to changes in neurofilaments, which are examples of which cytoskeletal filament type?
questions.e: Neurofilaments are a class of intermediate filament found in neurons; their disruption is a separate Alzheimer's mechanism from the tau/microtubule pathway.

questions.q: Roughly what percentage of the cytosol is water?
questions.e: The cytosol is approximately 75–90% water, with the remainder consisting of dissolved and suspended organic molecules and ions.

questions.q: What is the plasma membrane's basic composition?
o: A phospholipid bilayer plus associated membrane lipids and proteins
A rigid cellulose wall with embedded minerals, a plant cell-wall feature
A layer of carbohydrate surrounding the nucleus, not the plasma membrane
A single layer of protein only, with no lipid component at all
questions.e: The plasma membrane is the boundary membrane of the cell, made of a phospholipid bilayer together with associated membrane lipids and proteins.

questions.q: What is the cytosol?
o: Everything inside the plasma membrane except the nucleus
The aqueous portion of the cytoplasm outside all organelles
The lipid bilayer of the plasma membrane
questions.e: Cytosol is the aqueous cytoplasm that lies outside all the membrane-bound organelles; cytoplasm is everything outside the nucleus.

questions.q: Why does each organelle need its own biomembrane with a distinct protein complement?
o: To give the organelle a carbohydrate coat
To make the organelle heavier for centrifugation
To prevent the organelle from moving within the cytosol
questions.e: Each organelle's biomembrane carries a unique set of proteins that enable that organelle's specific functions, and forms a closed structure separating its lumen from the cytosol.

questions.q: According to the Fluid Mosaic Model, the membrane is best described as:
o: A solid protein sheet coated with lipid, rather than a fluid structure
A carbohydrate scaffold with no lipid component, which is not accurate
A rigid crystal lattice of proteins, the opposite of a fluid membrane
A fluid structure with a mosaic of proteins embedded within it
questions.e: The Fluid Mosaic Model describes the membrane as fluid, with a mosaic of various proteins embedded within the lipid bilayer.

questions.q: Which membrane lipid is described as amphipathic and is the most abundant?
questions.e: Phospholipids are the most abundant membrane lipid and are amphipathic, having both hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions.

questions.q: In the phospholipid bilayer, which part of each phospholipid faces the surrounding water?
questions.e: The polar hydrophilic heads face outward toward water on both sides of the membrane, while the hydrophobic tails face inward, away from water.

questions.q: In a phosphoglyceride, how many of glycerol's three hydroxyl groups are esterified to fatty acyl chains?
questions.e: Two of glycerol's three hydroxyl groups are esterified to fatty acyl chains; the third hydroxyl is esterified to a phosphate group.

questions.q: In a phosphoglyceride, what is esterified to the third hydroxyl group of glycerol?
questions.e: The third hydroxyl group of glycerol is esterified to a phosphate group, which forms the polar head of the phospholipid.

questions.q: How frequently do phospholipids typically move laterally within a membrane leaflet?
questions.e: Lateral movement of phospholipids within the bilayer is very frequent, occurring roughly 10⁷ times per second.

questions.q: How often does a given phospholipid undergo 'flip-flop' movement across the bilayer?
o: Several times per second, far faster than flip-flop actually occurs
About once per month, an intrinsically rare event
Continuously, at the same rate as lateral movement within the leaflet
About 10⁷ times per second, the rate of lateral movement instead
questions.e: Transverse flip-flop movement, where a phospholipid crosses from one leaflet to the other, is rare — occurring only about once per month.

questions.q: How does an unsaturated fatty acid tail affect membrane fluidity compared to a saturated one?
o: It converts the tail into a hydrophilic region, which double bonds do not do
It has no effect on fluidity, though kinks clearly change packing
It increases fluidity because kinks prevent tight packing
It decreases fluidity by packing more tightly, the saturated tail's effect
questions.e: Unsaturated tails contain kinks from double bonds that prevent tight packing, increasing membrane fluidity; saturated tails pack tightly and increase rigidity.

questions.q: What happens to a membrane's fluidity as temperature decreases?
o: Fluidity is unaffected by temperature, though cooling clearly changes it
Only glycolipids respond to temperature change, unlike other membrane lipids
It becomes more fluid, the opposite of what cooling actually causes
It shifts from a fluid state toward a more solid, rigid state overall
questions.e: As temperature cools, membranes shift from a fluid state toward a more solid state; the exact solidification temperature depends on lipid composition.

questions.q: A membrane rich in unsaturated fatty acids, compared with one rich in saturated fatty acids, will:
o: Stay fluid at a lower temperature
questions.e: Membranes rich in unsaturated fatty acids remain fluid at lower temperatures than membranes rich in saturated fatty acids.

questions.q: What does cholesterol do to membrane fluidity at warm temperatures around 37°C?
o: It has no effect at warm temperatures
It causes the membrane to become completely rigid
questions.e: At warm temperatures, cholesterol restrains excess phospholipid movement, moderating fluidity.

questions.q: What does cholesterol do to membrane fluidity at cool temperatures?
o: It removes glycolipids from the membrane
It has no effect at cool temperatures
It maintains fluidity by preventing tight lipid packing
It causes phospholipids to flip-flop more often
questions.e: At cool temperatures, cholesterol wedges between phospholipids and prevents them packing too tightly, maintaining fluidity.

questions.q: A protein that fully spans the membrane from one side to the other is specifically called:
o: A glycolipid, a lipid with an attached carbohydrate, not a spanning protein
A cholesterol-binding protein, a description unrelated to spanning the membrane
A peripheral protein, which does not fully span the membrane
A transmembrane protein, extending completely across the bilayer
questions.e: An integral protein that extends completely across the membrane is called a transmembrane protein.

questions.q: Integral membrane proteins are described as amphipathic because:
o: Their hydrophobic portions embed among the phospholipid tails while hydrophilic portions face the aqueous environment
They are entirely hydrophobic throughout, which would prevent any aqueous exposure at all
They dissolve completely in water everywhere, unlike a true membrane-embedded protein
They contain only hydrophilic amino acids throughout, with no hydrophobic segment present
questions.e: Integral proteins have hydrophobic segments embedded among the phospholipid tails, and hydrophilic segments exposed to the aqueous environment on either side.

questions.q: Which membrane protein type is attached to the membrane surface, not embedded, and is easily removed?
questions.e: Peripheral proteins attach to the inner or outer membrane surface, are not embedded in the bilayer, and can be removed relatively easily.

questions.q: What is the glycocalyx?
o: The cytoskeletal layer just inside the membrane, not the extracellular coat
The protein core of a transmembrane channel, not a carbohydrate coat
A carbohydrate coat formed by glycoproteins and glycolipids on the extracellular surface
The phosphate head of a phospholipid, a single lipid component, not a coat
questions.e: The glycocalyx is the carbohydrate coat, formed by glycoproteins and glycolipids, that gives a cell identity/uniqueness, aids cell-cell adhesion, and traps a slippery fluid layer.

questions.q: A membrane protein that binds a substance, changes shape, and moves it across the membrane is functioning as a:
o: Receptor protein, which binds a signal without transporting it across
Structural cytoskeletal protein, which anchors filaments rather than transporting
Channel protein, which forms a pore rather than changing shape to carry cargo
Transporter protein, which binds, changes shape, and carries cargo across
questions.e: Transporter proteins bind a substance, undergo a conformational change, and move the substance across the membrane.

questions.q: A membrane protein that forms a passageway allowing specific substances to cross is functioning as a:
questions.e: Channel-forming proteins create passageways through which specific substances can cross the membrane.

questions.q: Which of these can diffuse directly across the lipid bilayer without a protein channel?
o: Na⁺ ions, which actually require a channel or transporter to cross
O₂ and CO₂, small non-polar molecules that pass straight through
Large macromolecules such as proteins, which require vesicular transport
Glucose, which actually requires a transporter protein to cross
questions.e: Small non-polar/uncharged molecules such as O₂ and CO₂, along with steroids, can diffuse directly through the lipid bilayer.

questions.q: How does water typically cross the plasma membrane through the lipid bilayer itself?
o: It cannot cross the lipid bilayer at all, though some water does pass through
Through permanent large pores, which the bilayer does not actually contain
Through transient gaps that open as phospholipids move
By binding cholesterol and being carried across, which is not the mechanism
questions.e: Water can pass through transient gaps that open momentarily as phospholipids move within the bilayer.

questions.q: How do macromolecules typically cross the plasma membrane?
o: Through flip-flop movement of the macromolecule, which does not occur this way
By diffusing directly through the lipid bilayer, which macromolecules cannot do
Through simple channel proteins, which are too narrow for macromolecules
Via vesicular transport, such as endocytosis or exocytosis of the cargo
questions.e: Macromolecules cannot cross the membrane directly and require vesicular transport, such as endocytosis or exocytosis.

questions.q: Small polar and charged particles typically cross the membrane via:
o: Transmembrane channel/transporter proteins that let charged particles cross
Flip-flop movement, a mechanism that applies to lipids, not charged particles
Dissolving in the glycocalyx, which does not move particles across the membrane
Direct diffusion through the lipid tails, which polar particles cannot do
questions.e: Because the lipid bilayer is not directly permeable to charged/polar particles, transmembrane proteins act as channels or transporters for them.

questions.q: Which ion/molecule is typically found in higher concentration OUTSIDE the cell?
questions.e: There is typically more O₂ and Na⁺ outside the cell, while CO₂ and K⁺ are typically more concentrated inside the cell.

questions.q: An electrical gradient (membrane potential) refers to:
o: The rate of phospholipid flip-flop, a fluidity property, not an electrical one
A difference in temperature across the membrane, not an electrical property
A difference in charged ion distribution inside versus outside the cell
A difference in lipid saturation across the bilayer, a fluidity property instead
questions.e: The electrical gradient, or membrane potential, is the difference in the distribution of charged ions inside versus outside the cell.

questions.q: Substances generally move down their concentration gradient and:
o: Only when a receptor protein is present
questions.e: Substances move down concentration gradients and, if charged, toward oppositely charged regions — together forming an electrochemical gradient.

questions.q: What is the purpose of cell fractionation?
o: To investigate organelle function by disrupting cells and separating them into components
To measure the pH of the cytosol, which is not the purpose of fractionation
To grow more cells in culture, an unrelated laboratory technique entirely
To stain organelles for microscopy, a separate preparation technique altogether
questions.e: Cell fractionation disrupts cells and separates them into components in order to investigate organelle function.

questions.q: What are the three steps of cell fractionation, in order?
o: Analysis, fractionation, disruption, the reverse of the correct order
Centrifugation, staining, microscopy, steps that do not describe fractionation
Fixation, sectioning, staining, steps used for microscopy preparation instead
questions.e: Cell fractionation proceeds through disruption/homogenisation (producing a homogenate), fractionation/separation of the components, and finally analysis of their chemical activity.

questions.q: Why is homogenisation performed in an iso-osmotic medium?
o: To activate DNase and RNase, which is not the reason for an iso-osmotic medium
To dissolve the plasma membrane completely, which would defeat the purpose
To prevent organelles from osmotically swelling or shrinking during disruption
To increase the density of all organelles equally, which osmolarity does not do
questions.e: An iso-osmotic medium helps keep organelles intact (not osmotically bursting or shrinking) while the cell itself is being disrupted.

questions.q: Which liquid homogenisation device uses a manual glass pestle inside a glass tube?
questions.e: The Dounce homogenizer uses a manual glass pestle within a glass tube to shear cell membranes.

questions.q: Which liquid homogenisation device uses a Teflon pestle in a conical vessel, and can be manual or mechanical?
questions.e: The Potter-Elvehjem homogenizer uses a Teflon pestle within a conical vessel, and can be operated manually or mechanically.

questions.q: Which homogenisation method uses a piston to force a sample through a tiny hole under high pressure, and is preferred for bacterial cells?
questions.e: The French press forces samples of 40-250 ml through a tiny hole under high pressure, needs only 2 passes, and is the preferred (though expensive) method for breaking tough bacterial cells.

questions.q: Which homogenisation method is especially effective for releasing recombinant proteins from bacteria and relies on ice-crystal formation over multiple cycles?
questions.e: Freeze and thaw cycles form ice crystals that swell and break cells; multiple cycles are typically needed, and it is effective for releasing recombinant proteins from bacteria.

questions.q: Which homogenisation method is most common for plant cells, and is typically done after freezing tissue in liquid nitrogen?
questions.e: Mortar and pestle, used after freezing tissue in liquid nitrogen, is the most common method for plant cells and the fastest way to access proteins/DNA given the strength of the cellulose wall.

questions.q: Which additive promotes cell swelling and bursting during homogenisation?
questions.e: Hypotonic buffers cause water to enter cells, promoting swelling and eventual bursting during homogenisation.

questions.q: Which additive is used to digest the polysaccharide cell walls of yeast or bacteria before lysis (at roughly 200 µg/ml)?
questions.e: Enzyme digestion at around 200 µg/ml is used to break down the polysaccharide cell walls of yeast and bacteria.

questions.q: What is the role of protease inhibitors added during homogenisation?
o: To facilitate crushing of yeast cells
To prevent proteolysis of released proteins
To reduce the viscosity of nucleic acids
questions.e: Protease inhibitors prevent proteolysis, protecting released proteins from being degraded by cellular proteases during and after lysis.

questions.q: What two factors, besides particle size, affect sedimentation rate during centrifugation?
o: pH and viscosity of the buffer only
questions.e: Sedimentation rate during centrifugation depends on particle size, density and shape.

questions.q: In differential centrifugation, what does 'differential' refer to?
o: Repeated centrifugation at increasing centrifugal force to separate by size
A single spin that separates everything simultaneously, the opposite of differential
Comparing two different cell types, unrelated to what 'differential' means here
Different buffers used for each organelle, which is not the actual meaning
questions.e: Differential centrifugation uses repeated centrifugations at increasing centrifugal force, separating particles primarily by size into pellet and supernatant at each step.

questions.q: After a differential centrifugation spin, what is the 'pellet'?
o: The smaller structures suspended in the liquid, which describes the supernatant instead
The larger, denser structures collected at the bottom of the tube
The liquid layer above the sediment, which is actually the supernatant
The gradient medium used for the spin, not the sedimented material itself
questions.e: The pellet consists of the larger structures that sediment to the bottom of the tube, while the supernatant contains the smaller, still-suspended components.

questions.q: In the example protocol, what pellets when a homogenate is centrifuged at 1000×g for 10 minutes?
questions.e: At the low speed of 1000×g for 10 minutes, only the largest, densest structures — unbroken cells and heavy nuclei — pellet out.

questions.q: Why is repeated washing, re-suspension and re-pelleting in isotonic solvents performed after a differential spin?
o: To stain the pellet for microscopy, an unrelated preparation step entirely
To convert the pellet into a supernatant, which washing does not actually do
To fully dissolve the organelles, which would defeat the purpose of purification
To remove smaller contaminants, as a preliminary step before density-gradient separation
questions.e: Repeated washing/re-suspension/re-pelleting removes smaller contaminants from the pellet and serves as a preliminary step before finer density-gradient purification.

questions.q: Density gradient centrifugation is generally considered:
o: The preferred method for purifying subcellular organelles and macromolecules
Obsolete and replaced entirely by differential centrifugation, which is not the case
Only usable for separating viruses, a description far narrower than its real use
A crude first step only, never used for purification, unlike its actual role
questions.e: Density gradient (buoyant density) centrifugation is the preferred method for purifying subcellular organelles or macromolecules.

questions.q: In a sucrose density gradient, how are the layers typically arranged?
o: Lightest at the bottom, heaviest at the top
Heaviest at the bottom, lightest at the top
questions.e: Sucrose density gradients are layered with the heaviest medium at the bottom and the lightest at the top, either as discontinuous steps or a continuous gradient.

questions.q: Rate-zonal centrifugation separates particles mainly on the basis of:
o: Size/mass, even when density is similar
questions.e: Rate-zonal separation exploits differences in particle size/mass rather than density — useful, for example, for separating endosomes or antibody classes of similar density but different mass.

questions.q: What is the classic example of isopycnic separation described in the technique's use for nucleic acids?
o: Caesium chloride gradient for nucleic acids
questions.e: The classic example of isopycnic (density/equilibrium) separation is separating nucleic acids in a caesium chloride (CsCl) gradient.

questions.q: The analytical ultracentrifuge relies on which underlying principle?
o: Mass and gravitational laws, requiring no comparison standards
Electrical charge of particles only, not the principle it actually relies on
Enzymatic digestion of the sample, unrelated to how this instrument works
Fluorescent tagging of organelles, a technique this instrument does not use
questions.e: The analytical ultracentrifuge is a classical method relying on mass and gravitational laws, and it requires no comparison standards.

questions.q: A spectrophotometer is best described as a combination of which two devices?
o: A cuvette and a galvanometer only
questions.e: A spectrophotometer combines a spectrometer, which produces light of a selected wavelength, with a photometer, which measures light intensity.

questions.q: In a spectrophotometer, what holds the liquid sample between the spectrometer and photometer?
o: A silver halide emulsion, a component of autoradiography film instead
A quartz cell used only in ultracentrifugation, not spectrophotometry
A cuvette, the small vessel holding sample in the light path
A sucrose gradient tube, a component of density-gradient centrifugation instead
questions.e: A cuvette holds the liquid sample in the light path between the spectrometer and the photometer.

questions.q: What does autoradiography primarily visualise?
o: The lipid saturation of the plasma membrane, which autoradiography does not visualise
The molecular weight of a purified protein, a property this technique does not show
The pH distribution across a membrane, which is not what this technique visualises
The distribution of radioactively labelled substances within tissue, cells or biomolecules
questions.e: Autoradiography visualises the distribution of radioactively labelled substances within tissue, cells, organelles or biomolecules, and allows quantitative estimation by densitometry.

questions.q: In autoradiography, what ultimately forms the dark bands seen on the developed film?
o: Reduced silver atoms from activated silver halide crystals
Deposited sucrose crystals, which do not form the dark bands seen on the film
Stained DNase enzymes, which play no part in forming autoradiography bands
Condensed water vapour, which is not responsible for the dark bands seen
questions.e: Radioactive emissions activate silver halide crystals in the photographic emulsion; the resulting Ag⁺ ions are reduced to metallic Ag atoms, forming the dark bands.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a commonly used isotope in autoradiography?
questions.e: Commonly used autoradiography isotopes include tritium (³H), ¹⁴C, ³²P, ⁴⁵Ca and ³⁵S; technetium-99m is not among the listed isotopes.

questions.q: In partition chromatography, the stationary phase is a:
o: Gel, relying on molecular size exclusion, the mechanism of gel filtration instead
Solid, relying on electrostatic interactions, the mechanism of adsorption chromatography
Liquid, relying on relative solubility between immiscible solvents
Gas, relying on diffusion rate, a description that does not fit this technique
questions.e: In partition chromatography, the stationary phase is a liquid, and separation depends on the relative solubility of components between two or more immiscible solvents (the partition coefficient).

questions.q: In adsorption chromatography, the stationary phase is a:
o: Gas, relying on temperature, which does not describe the stationary phase here
Liquid, relying on pH alone, which does not describe adsorption chromatography
Liquid, relying on solubility, the mechanism of partition chromatography instead
Solid, relying mainly on electrostatic interactions with the solute molecules
questions.e: In adsorption chromatography, the stationary phase is a solid, and separation relies mainly on electrostatic interactions between the solute and the solid surface.

questions.q: In paper chromatography, how does the solvent move up the paper carrying the sample with it?
questions.e: The solvent rises up the paper via capillary action, carrying the sample components with it at different rates.

questions.q: In column chromatography, if solute B has a lower affinity for the stationary phase than solute A, what happens?
o: Both solutes elute simultaneously regardless of affinity, which is not the case
Solute B remains permanently bound to the column, which is not what happens
Solute B elutes from the column before solute A, since it binds more weakly
Solute A elutes before solute B, the reverse of what lower affinity produces
questions.e: Because solute B has a lower affinity for the stationary phase, it migrates faster down the column and emerges (elutes) before solute A, which is retained longer.

questions.q: Which two solvent conditions can be varied in column chromatography to alter separation and elution timing?
questions.e: The pH and temperature of the solvent can be varied in column chromatography to change how solutes separate and when they elute.

questions.q: What does the numerical aperture of a lens primarily describe?
questions.e: Numerical aperture combines the refractive index of the medium and the half-angle of the light cone accepted by the lens.

questions.q: Total magnification of a microscope is calculated by:
questions.e: Total magnification = objective magnification × eyepiece magnification.

questions.q: Which optical defect causes different wavelengths of light to focus at different points?
questions.e: Chromatic aberration arises because a simple lens bends different wavelengths of light by different amounts.

questions.q: Immersion oil is used with certain objectives primarily to:
o: Increase resolution by matching refractive indices
questions.e: Immersion oil has a refractive index close to glass, reducing light refraction/loss and improving resolution.

questions.q: "Empty magnification" refers to:
o: Magnifying beyond the resolving power without gaining detail
questions.e: Once the resolution limit is reached, further magnification just enlarges a blurry image without revealing new detail.

questions.q: Which component controls the amount of light reaching the specimen?
questions.e: The condenser and its iris diaphragm regulate and focus the light illuminating the specimen.

questions.q: A parfocal microscope is one where:
o: The specimen stays roughly in focus when switching objectives
The specimen stays centered when switching objectives
Both eyepieces show the same image
questions.e: Parfocal design means only minor focus adjustment is needed after changing magnification.

questions.q: Which factor most directly limits the resolution of a standard light microscope?
o: The thickness of the glass slide
questions.e: Diffraction of light, governed by its wavelength, sets the fundamental resolution limit (~200 nm) of light microscopy.

questions.q: Which microscopy technique is best suited to observing unstained, living cells with enhanced contrast?
questions.e: Phase-contrast microscopy converts subtle differences in refractive index into visible contrast, without staining or killing the cell.

questions.q: TEM produces images by:
o: Passing electrons through an ultrathin specimen
Using visible light through a specimen
questions.e: Transmission electron microscopy relies on electrons passing through a very thin section, with denser areas scattering more electrons.

questions.q: SEM is most useful for studying:
questions.e: Scanning electron microscopy scans a beam over the specimen surface, producing detailed 3D-like topographic images.

questions.q: Why must electron microscopy be performed in a vacuum?
o: Air molecules would scatter the electron beam
questions.e: Electrons are easily scattered by air molecules, so a vacuum is required to allow the beam to travel undisturbed to the specimen.

questions.q: Heavy metal stains such as osmium tetroxide are used in EM to:
o: Increase contrast by scattering electrons more strongly
questions.e: Because EM images are formed by electron scattering (not light absorption), heavy metals are used to create contrast.

questions.q: The Gram stain is used to classify bacteria based on:
o: Differences in their cell wall structure
questions.e: Gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria retain or lose the crystal violet stain differently based on peptidoglycan layer thickness.

questions.q: Freeze-fracture technique is primarily used to reveal:
questions.e: Freeze-fracture splits a frozen membrane along its hydrophobic core, exposing internal membrane faces for study.

questions.q: Which of the following best distinguishes cryo-electron microscopy from standard TEM?
o: Specimens are rapidly frozen to preserve near-native structure without staining
It uses visible light instead of electrons
questions.e: Cryo-EM images vitrified, hydrated specimens, avoiding artifacts introduced by chemical fixation and staining.

questions.q: Which feature is unique to eukaryotic cells and absent in prokaryotic cells?
questions.e: Eukaryotic cells possess a true, membrane-enclosed nucleus, while prokaryotic DNA is concentrated in an unbound nucleoid region.

questions.q: According to endosymbiotic theory, mitochondria most likely originated from:
o: A piece of the cell wall
questions.e: Endosymbiotic theory proposes mitochondria arose from a free-living aerobic bacterium engulfed by an ancestral host cell.

questions.q: Prokaryotic ribosomes are classified as:
questions.e: Prokaryotic ribosomes have a sedimentation coefficient of 70S, smaller than the 80S ribosomes of eukaryotes.

questions.q: A bacterial plasmid is best described as:
o: A small circular DNA molecule separate from the main chromosome
questions.e: Plasmids often carry accessory genes, such as antibiotic resistance, and replicate independently of the main chromosome.

questions.q: Which reproductive method is characteristic of prokaryotic cells?
questions.e: Prokaryotes reproduce asexually through binary fission, a simpler process than eukaryotic mitosis.

questions.q: Peptidoglycan is a key structural component of:
questions.e: Peptidoglycan, a polymer of sugars and amino acids, forms the rigid structural layer of most bacterial cell walls.

questions.q: Which domain of life consists exclusively of prokaryotic organisms with distinct biochemistry from bacteria?
questions.e: Archaea are prokaryotic but biochemically and genetically distinct from Bacteria, forming their own domain.

questions.q: As a cell increases in size, its surface area to volume ratio:
questions.e: Volume grows faster than surface area as size increases, eventually limiting a cell's ability to exchange materials efficiently.

questions.q: The primary function of mitochondria is to:
questions.e: Mitochondria generate the majority of a eukaryotic cell's ATP via aerobic cellular respiration.

questions.q: Which organelle is primarily responsible for modifying, sorting, and packaging proteins for secretion?
questions.e: The Golgi apparatus receives proteins from the ER and processes them before directing them to their final destinations.

questions.q: Lysosomes contain which type of enzymes?
questions.e: Lysosomes house hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes that break down macromolecules, damaged organelles, and waste.

questions.q: Rough endoplasmic reticulum differs from smooth ER in that it:
o: Is studded with ribosomes for protein synthesis
questions.e: The ribosomes attached to rough ER carry out translation of proteins destined for secretion or membrane insertion.

questions.q: Microtubules are cytoskeletal filaments composed of:
questions.e: Microtubules are polymers of the protein tubulin and play roles in transport, structure, and cell division.

questions.q: Peroxisomes are primarily responsible for:
o: Breaking down fatty acids and detoxifying hydrogen peroxide
questions.e: Peroxisomes contain oxidative enzymes, including catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide generated during fatty acid oxidation.

questions.q: Which structure organizes microtubules during animal cell division?
questions.e: The centrosome, containing a pair of centrioles, serves as the main microtubule-organizing center in animal cells.

questions.q: The process by which a cell degrades and recycles its own damaged organelles is called:
questions.e: Autophagy uses double-membraned autophagosomes to engulf damaged components and deliver them to lysosomes for degradation.

questions.q: The fluid mosaic model describes the plasma membrane as:
o: A fluid lipid bilayer with embedded, mobile proteins
A rigid, solid layer of protein
questions.e: This model reflects the membrane's fluid nature, with proteins and lipids able to move laterally within the bilayer.

questions.q: Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion in that it:
o: Requires a channel or carrier protein
questions.e: Facilitated diffusion is still passive (no ATP needed) but relies on specific membrane transport proteins to move molecules.

questions.q: A cell placed in a hypertonic solution will typically:
questions.e: In a hypertonic solution, water moves out of the cell toward the higher external solute concentration, causing shrinkage.

questions.q: The sodium-potassium pump is an example of:
questions.e: This pump directly uses ATP hydrolysis to move sodium and potassium ions against their concentration gradients.

questions.q: In differential centrifugation, which cellular component is typically pelleted first, at the lowest speed?
questions.e: Larger, denser structures like nuclei and unbroken cells sediment first at low centrifugal speeds.

questions.q: Cell fractionation typically begins with which step?
o: Homogenization to break open the cells
questions.e: Homogenization physically disrupts the cells, releasing their contents into a solution before any centrifugation occurs.

questions.q: Glycoproteins on the outer surface of the plasma membrane primarily function in:
questions.e: Carbohydrate chains attached to membrane proteins form part of the glycocalyx, important for cell-cell recognition.

questions.q: Cholesterol embedded in animal cell membranes primarily functions to:
questions.e: Cholesterol interacts with phospholipids to stabilize membrane fluidity across a range of temperatures.

questions.q: In distinguishing between limit of resolution and resolving power, which of the following statement is not true?
o: Limit of resolution is the minimum distance between two points that can still be resolved
Limit of resolution of light microscope is 240nm
Resolving power is dependent on wave length of light
Resolving power of light microscope may be improved by blue light
questions.e: This describes resolving power's inverse, not limit of resolution directly — as marked in the source paper.

questions.q: The approximate wavelength of electrons over a potential difference of V volts can be calculated from the equation λ = √(1.5/V) nm. At 100 KV will have an apparent wavelength of?
What is the name and function of the mirror labelled A in Fig. 1 (a fluorescence microscope diagram)?
o: Emission filter, filters the green light
Emission filter, filters the emission light from the chromogenic molecules
Dichroic mirror that filters emission from the sample
Excitation filter, filters the fluorescence emitted from the sample
questions.e: Mirror A sits at the beam-splitting angle between the light source and the sample/detector path — the position of a dichroic mirror, which reflects excitation light down to the sample and passes emitted light up to the detector.

questions.q: What is the name and function of the mirror labelled B in Fig. 1?
o: Emission filter, filters the green light
Emission filter, filters the emission light from the chromogenic molecules
Dichroic mirror that filters emission from the sample
Excitation filter, filters the fluorescence emitted from the sample
questions.e: Mirror B sits between the lamp and the dichroic mirror, in the excitation light path — the position of the excitation filter.

questions.q: What is the name and function of the mirror labelled C in Fig. 1?
o: Emission filter, filters the green light
Emission filter, filters the emission light from the chromogenic molecules
Dichroic mirror that filters emission from the sample
Emission filter, filters the fluorescence emitted from the sample
questions.e: Mirror C sits between the dichroic mirror and the detector, in the emitted-light path — the position of the emission filter, which isolates the fluorescence from the chromogenic molecules.

questions.q: Which would be the best choice for viewing internal structures of a living amoeba?
questions.e: Phase contrast reveals internal detail in living, unstained, transparent cells by turning small refractive-index differences into contrast — a stain or EM fixation would kill the amoeba.

questions.q: What is the limit of resolution of the light microscope using green light of wavelength 560 nm, given the numerical aperture to be 1.4?
questions.e: Using the Rayleigh criterion, resolution ≈ 0.61λ/NA = 0.61(560)/1.4 ≈ 244 nm, which rounds to about 240nm.

questions.q: What is the difference between a Bright-field and Dark-field microscopy?
o: Bright-field is a simple mic, but a Dark-field is compound microscope
Bright-field has an opaque disc in the substage condenser but not Dark-field
A bright image in a dark background is seen in Dark-field microscope but bright-field in addition has a bright background
There is more contrast in bright-field as compared to Dark-field
questions.e: Dark-field blocks the direct light so only scattered light from the specimen reaches the eye (bright specimen, dark background), while bright-field illuminates the whole field evenly.

questions.q: Resolving power of a microscope is a function of
o: wavelength of light used and numerical aperture of lens system
questions.e: Resolving power depends on both the wavelength of light used and the numerical aperture of the lens system (resolution ≈ 0.61λ/NA).

questions.q: The longer the working distance….
questions.e: A longer working distance goes with a lower-power, lower-NA, narrower-aperture objective, which gives a smaller image — as marked in the source paper.

questions.q: The apparent size of an image divided by its real size.
questions.e: This is the definition of magnification.

questions.q: The minimum distance between two points that can still be seen as distinct structures.
questions.e: This is the definition of resolution.

questions.q: The difference between the brightness of various parts of the specimen compared to that of the background
questions.e: This describes contrast — as marked in the source paper (note the options here omit "Contrast" itself).

questions.q: Microfilaments are composed of a protein called ______
questions.e: Microfilaments (part of the cytoskeleton) are polymers of the protein actin.

questions.q: Part of the microscope on which the object of investigation is positioned.
questions.e: The specimen (or stage) is the platform that holds the slide under the objective lens.

questions.q: In electron microscopy, which of the following is used as a fixative prior to staining technique?
questions.e: Glutaraldehyde is a standard chemical fixative used to preserve ultrastructure before EM staining (uranium salts are used later, as a stain).

questions.q: The shorter the focal length of the lens;
o: the higher the contrast of the microscope
Cannot be determined from the statement
questions.e: A shorter focal length allows a higher numerical aperture, which increases resolving power.

questions.q: What is the essence of the UV light microscope having a photographic screen to capture image?
o: UV light rays cannot form images
UV light may damage the eyes
UV light produces higher resolution which cannot be seen by the naked eyes
questions.e: UV light gives finer resolution than visible light, but because it's invisible to the human eye, the image must be captured on a photographic (or equivalent) screen instead of viewed directly.

questions.q: Generally bright-field microscopy is not well suited for live specimen why?
o: Because light rays are not refracted efficiently by the organisms
Because the diffraction pattern of the image forming rays cannot be distinguished
Because the specimen background reflects light
Because of poor contrast due to similar light intensities in the specimen and the background
questions.e: Unstained living cells are mostly transparent, so in bright-field the specimen and background transmit similar amounts of light, giving very poor contrast.

questions.q: (Table 1, Statement I) “Light rays passing through a lens near its horizontal axis are refracted less than rays closer to the edge or periphery of the lens and as a result, end up in different spots across the optical axis.” This statement is a description of?
questions.e: Rays passing through different radial zones of a spherical lens focusing at different points along the axis is the definition of spherical aberration.

questions.q: (Table 1, Statement II) “Parallel rays of light do not converge at the focal point.” This statement is a description of?
questions.e: Failing to converge parallel rays at a single focal point is a direct consequence of spherical aberration.

questions.q: (Table 1, Statement III) “The specimen stays in focus with varying working distance.” This statement is a description of?
questions.e: A parfocal system keeps the specimen in focus even as the effective working distance/objective changes.

questions.q: (Table 1, Statement III, repeated) “The specimen stays in focus with varying working distance.” This statement is a description of?
questions.e: As in the previous question, this is the definition of parfocal focusing.

questions.q: (Table 1, Statement V) “A spectrum of wavelength within visible light are not brought to a simultaneous focus.” This statement is a description of?
o: Chromatic aberration — none of the printed choices names it correctly
questions.e: Different wavelengths (colours) of light focusing at different points is, by definition, chromatic aberration — the source paper's own answer key flags that none of its printed options state this correctly.

questions.q: (Table 1, Statement IV) “Blurred images are formed because light rays from a specimen are not brought to simultaneous focus.” This statement is a description of?
questions.e: Light rays from a single point on the specimen failing to reach a simultaneous, sharp focus is spherical aberration, which blurs the image.

questions.q: The fluidity of the plasma membrane increases with increase in ______.
o: saturated fatty acids in the membrane
unsaturated fatty acids in the membrane
questions.e: Unsaturated fatty acid tails have kinks that prevent tight packing, keeping the membrane more fluid; saturated tails pack tightly and reduce fluidity.

questions.q: The function of the centrosome is ______
questions.e: The centrosome organizes microtubules and is the main site of spindle fibre formation during cell division.

questions.q: Which cell organelle is involved in apoptosis?
questions.e: Mitochondria release cytochrome c and trigger the caspase cascade central to programmed cell death (apoptosis).

questions.q: 10 Angstrom (Å) as a unit of measurement is equal to
questions.e: 1 Å = 0.1 nm, so 10 Å = 1 nm.

questions.q: Spherical aberration occurs when
o: the light intensity is too high
when light rays are not brought to a sharp focus
when light rays through the lens do not converge at the same focal point
questions.e: Spherical aberration is when rays passing through different parts of a lens fail to converge at one common focal point.

questions.q: Which optical aberration is corrected by introduction of glycerol/oil as the imaging medium?
questions.e: Oil (or glycerol) immersion matches the refractive index between the slide and the lens, reducing the spherical aberration that would otherwise occur from refraction at the glass–air interface.

questions.q: What is the range of the electromagnetic spectrum of visible light. It is from _____ to _____?
questions.e: The visible light spectrum is conventionally given as roughly 390–700 nm.

questions.q: A lens that is set to parfocal
o: stays in focus even when the objectives are changed
specimen remains in focus when the working distance is changed
when an opaque disc is inserted in the diaphragm
questions.e: Parfocal means the specimen stays in focus when you switch between objective lenses of different power.

questions.q: At very high magnifications with transmitted light, point objects are seen as fuzzy discs surrounded by diffraction rings. These are called
questions.e: These diffraction-limited fuzzy discs with surrounding rings are called Airy discs.

questions.q: Which of these statements is not true about numerical aperture?
o: It is directly proportional to refractive index
It is directly proportional to the angle of incidence illumination
Increasing the numerical aperture increases the resolving power of the microscope,
The numerical aperture is limited by visible light
questions.e: As marked in the source paper.

questions.q: Which microscope uses a dichroic mirror?
questions.e: The dichroic mirror is a defining component of the fluorescence microscope, reflecting excitation light to the sample and passing emitted light to the detector.

questions.q: The UV-Fluorescent microscopy may have better resolution than the bright-field microscopy due to the .......?
o: Dichroic mirror that filters blue light
Excitation of fluorescence species in the specimen
The photographic screen that captures the image
The shorter wave-length of UV light
questions.e: Resolution improves with shorter wavelength (resolution ≈ 0.61λ/NA), and UV light has a shorter wavelength than visible light.

questions.q: The UV-Fluorescent microscopy may have better contrast than the bright-field microscopy due to the .......?
o: Excitation of fluorescence species in the specimen
The photographic screen that captures the image
The shorter wave-length of UV light
The colors in the lenses are always brighter than the specimen
questions.e: Only the fluorescently-labelled structures emit light against an otherwise dark background, giving very high contrast.

questions.q: The ratio of the final image size to its actual size is ...
questions.e: This is the definition of magnification.

questions.q: The minimum distance between two points that can still be seen as distinct structures. (repeated)
questions.e: This is the definition of resolution.

questions.q: The difference between the brightness of various parts of the specimen compared to that of its background. (repeated)
questions.e: This is the definition of contrast.

questions.q: Which of the following microscopy techniques relies on the specimen interfering with the wavelength of light to produce a high contrast image without the need for stains or any damage to the sample?
questions.e: Phase contrast converts phase shifts caused by the specimen's refractive index (an interference effect) into visible contrast, without stains or damage.

questions.q: A white powder suspected of containing highly refractive Anthrax spores may be best imaged microscopically using what microscope technique?
questions.e: Phase contrast microscopy is well suited to highly refractive, unstained structures like bacterial spores.

questions.q: What is defined as the ability to see two neighboring points in a field as distinct entities?
questions.e: This is the definition of resolution.

questions.q: For an objective lens designed for use in air, what is the largest theoretically possible numerical aperture?
questions.e: NA = n·sin(θ). In air, n=1 and sin(θ) approaches but cannot exceed 1, so the theoretical maximum NA in air is 1.0 (in practice, oil-immersion lenses exceed this using a higher-index medium).

questions.q: The absorbance of visible light or UV light by a compound and the subsequent release by that compound of longer wavelength light is known as ______.
questions.e: Absorbing light and immediately re-emitting it at a longer wavelength is the definition of fluorescence.

questions.q: The Dark-field microscope is used to examine all the following specimen except;
o: specimen that is invisible in the ordinary light microscope,
cannot be stained by standard methods,
questions.e: Dark-field is used for unstained, invisible, or living specimens seen by scattered light — inherently fluorescent specimens are instead the domain of fluorescence microscopy.

questions.q: Instead of the normal condenser, the Dark-field microscope uses a dark-field condenser that contains ………….
questions.e: A dark-field condenser has an opaque central stop (disc) that blocks direct light, letting only obliquely scattered light reach the specimen and objective.

questions.q: The main technique exploited by the phase-contrast microscope to improve contrast is
o: differences in wave length of light,
differences in the incident angle of illumination
questions.e: Phase contrast converts small differences in refractive index (and thickness) within the specimen into visible differences in brightness.

questions.q: This cell is the longest in the human body.
questions.e: Certain nerve cells (e.g. those running down the sciatic nerve) can be roughly a metre long, making them the longest cells in the human body.

questions.q: Why are specimens fixed?
questions.e: Fixation is done to preserve the specimen's structure, halting decay and cell processes so it can be studied later.

questions.q: The Cell theory is not applicable to
questions.e: Cell theory states all living things are made of cells; viruses are not made of cells (they are acellular), so the theory does not apply to them.

questions.q: All the following statements are true about the phase contrast microscope except?
o: It is used to observe living cells,
Uses both transmitted light and scattered light
Overcomes the limitations of wavelength of visible light
questions.e: Phase contrast improves contrast using refractive-index differences, but it does not change or overcome the fundamental wavelength-based limit on resolution.

questions.q: From the following list, choose the correct order in which light passes through a dissecting microscope.
questions.e: Light reflects up from the mirror, through the slide/specimen, through the objective lens, and finally through the eyepiece to the eye.

questions.q: This is manipulated to bring the object being viewed closer.
questions.e: The focus knob moves the stage or objective to bring the specimen into sharp focus.

questions.q: In every organism its cells are different based on ______.
o: how they are positioned on the microscope
questions.e: Cells specialize according to their internal organization (which organelles they contain and how they're arranged), which is what gives rise to different cell types.

questions.q: An ant is 8cm as drawn in a class one homework book and the scale shows it to be 2mm in real life, what is its magnification?
questions.e: Magnification = drawn size / actual size = 8cm / 0.2cm = 40.

questions.q: Resolving power of a microscope is a function of ______. (repeated)
o: wavelength of light used and numerical aperture of lens system
questions.e: Resolving power depends on both the wavelength of light used and the numerical aperture of the lens system.

questions.q: When looking at specimen under a microscope, a thin slice of specimen is placed on a slide, a small drop of dye is placed on the tissue. What should be done next?
o: A coverslip is placed over the tissue
A drawing of the cells of the specimen
The coarse focus is adjusted until the cells become visible
The specimen is cut into thin slices
questions.e: After staining, a coverslip is placed over the tissue to protect it and flatten the sample before viewing.

questions.q: When the power of ocular lens is 10X and objective lens is 20x, the magnification is
questions.e: Total magnification = ocular × objective = 10 × 20 = 200X.

questions.q: All the following characteristics define life EXCEPT:
questions.e: A nucleus is exclusive to eukaryotic cells — prokaryotes are alive without one — so possessing a nucleus is not a universal defining characteristic of life.

questions.q: A difference between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells is having a:
questions.e: Both cell types can have ribosomes and (in many cases) a cell wall, but only eukaryotic cells have a true membrane-bound nucleus.

questions.q: Which of the following acts as a packaging and processing centre in the cell to process proteins?
questions.e: The Golgi body/apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins received from the ER before shipping them to their destinations.

questions.q: The central control unit of the cell is the:
questions.e: The nucleus houses the cell's DNA and directs gene expression, earning it the title of the cell's control centre.

questions.q: Ribosomes can be stationed on the rough endoplasmic reticulum. What is the role of this ribosome?
o: Modifies new polypeptide chains and synthesizes lipids
Supports moving the cell and its components
questions.e: Ribosomes — whether free or bound to the rough ER — are the sites of protein synthesis (translation).

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT found in plant cells?
questions.e: Plant cells lack centrioles/centrosomes; they organize their spindle apparatus without them, unlike animal cells.

questions.q: The limit of resolution of the unaided human eye is approximately:
questions.e: As reflected in the source material, the unaided human eye's limit of resolution is taken to be on the order of 1cm for this course.

questions.q: Which of the following has ribosomes attached to it and is a site for protein synthesis?
questions.e: The rough ER is studded with ribosomes on its cytosolic face, making it a major site of protein synthesis.

questions.q: The large, dark-staining spot within the nucleus which produces ribosomal subunits is the:
questions.e: The nucleolus is the dense nuclear region where ribosomal RNA is synthesized and assembled into ribosomal subunits.

questions.q: Which of the following is a sac-like structure that stores water in the cell?
questions.e: The (central) vacuole is the membrane-bound sac, especially prominent in plant cells, that stores water and maintains turgor pressure.

questions.q: The numerical aperture of an oil immersion objective is approximately:
questions.e: Oil immersion objectives are designed to achieve a high numerical aperture (commonly cited around 1.25–1.4) by matching the refractive index of the medium between specimen and lens with oil.

questions.q: The electromagnetic spectrum of visible light ranges from approximately:
questions.e: Visible light is conventionally defined as roughly 380-750nm, closest to the 390-700nm range given here.

questions.q: Lysosome vesicles actively participate in:
o: Regulating the movement of materials in and out of the cell
questions.e: Lysosomes release hydrolytic enzymes that help execute programmed cell death (apoptosis) alongside their digestive roles.

questions.q: In prokaryotes, the hair-like outgrowth that attaches bacterial cells to surfaces (or to other bacterial cells) is the:
questions.e: Pili are short, hair-like protein filaments on the bacterial surface used for attachment (and, for sex pili, conjugation).

questions.q: A sample of water taken from a hot thermal vent was found to contain a single-celled organism with a cell wall and no nucleus. It is most likely to be classified as:
questions.e: Extremophiles thriving in hot thermal vents, being prokaryotic (no nucleus) yet biochemically distinct from typical bacteria, are classically classified in the domain Archaea.

questions.q: The nucleus is essential in:
o: Moving the cell and its contents
Organizing the internal parts of the cell
questions.e: Among the options, organizing the internal parts of the cell best reflects the nucleus's role as the cell's control and organizing centre.

questions.q: The resolving power of a microscope depends on:
o: The focal length and aperture of the eye lens
The focal length and aperture of the objective lens
The aperture of the objective and eye lens
The wavelength of the light illuminating the object
questions.e: Resolving power is governed by the wavelength of illumination and the numerical aperture of the objective — shorter wavelengths and higher NA give finer resolution.

questions.q: Useful magnification is said to be achieved when:
o: The virtual image is 100x larger than the specimen
Two entities within the specimen can be rendered as separate and not as one
The specimen is enlarged and the entities within it can be resolved
The specimen is the same size as the image but all entities can be seen clearly
The specimen has been magnified to the maximum but entities are not rendered separate
questions.e: “Useful” magnification means the image is enlarged AND finer details are actually resolved — magnifying without resolving more detail is “empty” magnification.

questions.q: The optical aberration that is corrected by introducing glycerol as an imaging medium is:
questions.e: Matching the refractive index of the imaging medium (e.g. with glycerol) to the specimen/lens reduces spherical aberration caused by uneven ray bending at the interface.

questions.q: What is the numerical aperture of a microscope if the angle of incident light is 90° and the refractive index of the medium is 1.89?
questions.e: Numerical aperture NA = n·sin(θ). With θ = 90°, sin(θ) = 1, so NA = 1.89 × 1 = 1.89.

questions.q: The mammalian animal cell has all the following EXCEPT:
questions.e: Animal cells lack a rigid cell wall — that structure is characteristic of plant, fungal and bacterial cells, not mammalian cells.
